commands.title: Make the sound louder
commands.description: Increases the master volume by 5% using the ALSA sound mixer built into Linux. Run it multiple times to keep raising the volume. Takes effect immediately.

commands.title: Make the sound quieter
commands.description: Decreases the master volume by 5%. Run it multiple times to keep lowering the volume. No restart needed.

commands.title: Mute or unmute the sound
commands.description: Toggles the master volume mute on and off. If sound is playing and you run this, it will go silent. Run it again to bring the sound back.

commands.title: Set volume to a specific percentage
commands.description: Sets the master volume to exactly 70%. Change the number to any value between 0 (silent) and 100 (maximum). Useful when you want a precise volume level.

commands.title: List all audio output devices
commands.description: Shows all the sound output devices detected by your system, such as speakers, headphones, and HDMI audio. Useful to find the name of a device if sound is not working.

commands.title: List microphone and recording devices
commands.description: Shows all audio input devices detected by your system, such as built-in microphones and USB microphones. Use this to troubleshoot recording problems.

commands.title: Open the graphical volume control panel
commands.description: Opens PulseAudio Volume Control, a graphical app where you can control volume for each application separately, switch output devices, and manage microphones.

commands.title: Test if your speakers are working
commands.description: Plays a test sound through your speakers. You will hear audio in the left and right channels alternately. Press Ctrl+C to stop. Good for checking if audio is set up correctly.

commands.title: Restart the audio system (fixes no-sound problems)
commands.description: Kills and restarts PulseAudio, which is the sound server in Linux. This fixes most cases where sound suddenly stops working without rebooting the computer.

commands.title: Show audio system status and info
commands.description: Displays technical information about PulseAudio including the default input and output devices, sample rate, and server version. Useful for diagnosing audio issues.

commands.title: Take a screenshot of the whole screen
commands.description: Captures the entire screen and opens a dialog asking where to save it. The image is saved as a PNG file. You can also use the Print Screen key on your keyboard.

commands.title: Take a screenshot and save to a file
commands.description: Captures the entire screen and saves it immediately as a PNG file called screenshot.png in your home folder. No dialog box appears, so it is faster than the regular screenshot command.

commands.title: Take a screenshot of just one window
commands.description: Lets you click on any open window to capture only that window. A dialog then asks you where to save the image. Great for documenting a specific app.

commands.title: List all connected monitors and their settings
commands.description: Shows all the display outputs on your computer, which ones are active, and what resolution they are running at. Useful before changing screen settings.

commands.title: Lock the screen immediately
commands.description: Locks your screen right away, requiring your password to get back in. Useful when you are stepping away from the computer.

commands.title: Adjust screen brightness
commands.description: Sets the brightness of your main screen to 80% (0.8). Change the number between 0.1 (very dark) and 1.0 (full brightness). Replace eDP-1 with your display name from the xrandr command.

commands.title: Turn off an external monitor
commands.description: Turns off the monitor connected to HDMI. Replace HDMI-1 with the name of your output shown by the xrandr command. The monitor stays off until you reconnect it or change the setting.

commands.title: Show your computer's IP address on the local network
commands.description: Displays the IP address your computer has on your local network (home or office WiFi/ethernet). This is different from your public internet IP. Useful for connecting devices together.

commands.title: Show your public IP (what the internet sees)
commands.description: Asks a remote server what IP address your internet connection is using. This is the address websites see when you visit them. It comes from your router, not your computer directly.

commands.title: Check if a website or server is reachable
commands.description: Sends 4 test packets to google.com and measures how long they take to come back. If you get replies, your internet is working. If not, there may be a connection problem.

commands.title: Show WiFi and network connection status
commands.description: Lists all your network interfaces (WiFi, ethernet, etc.) and shows whether each one is connected, disconnected, or unavailable. A quick way to check your connection state.

commands.title: List all nearby WiFi networks
commands.description: Scans for nearby WiFi networks and shows their names (SSID), signal strength, and security type. Use this to find a network before connecting to it.

commands.title: Connect to a WiFi network
commands.description: Connects to a WiFi network by name and password. Replace NetworkName with the exact WiFi name and YourPassword with the password. Run in your terminal so you can type the password if needed.
commands.shell_only_reason: Connecting to WiFi may need your system password. Copy and run in terminal.

commands.title: Disconnect from WiFi
commands.description: Disconnects the WiFi adapter (wlan0) from any network. Replace wlan0 with your WiFi adapter name shown by the ip addr show command if yours is different.

commands.title: Download a file from the internet
commands.description: Downloads a file from a web address and saves it to your current folder. Replace the URL with the actual link to the file you want to download. Shows download progress as it runs.

commands.title: See all active network connections and open ports
commands.description: Lists all the network connections currently open on your computer, including which ports are listening for incoming connections. Useful for checking what services are running.

commands.title: Show all your network interfaces
commands.description: Lists all network adapters on your computer — WiFi, ethernet, loopback — along with their IP addresses and current state. More detailed than hostname -I.

commands.title: Show what folder you are in right now
commands.description: Prints the full path of the folder you are currently in. Useful when you are navigating in the terminal and lose track of where you are. PWD stands for Print Working Directory.

commands.title: List all files and folders in the current location
commands.description: Shows every file and folder in your current directory, including hidden files (those starting with a dot). The -la flags add file sizes, permissions, dates, and hidden files.

commands.title: Go to a specific folder
commands.description: Changes your current location to the folder you specify. For example, cd ~/Documents takes you to your Documents folder. The ~ symbol always means your home folder.
commands.shell_only_reason: cd changes the shell's location — it only works when run directly in your terminal.

commands.title: Create a new folder
commands.description: Creates a new empty folder with the name you specify. You can use a simple name like MyFolder or a full path like ~/Desktop/NewProject to create it somewhere specific.

commands.title: Create a new empty file
commands.description: Creates a new empty file with the name you choose. If the file already exists, it updates the modification date without changing the contents. Useful for quickly making a placeholder file.

commands.title: Delete a file permanently
commands.description: Permanently deletes a file. There is no trash or undo — the file is gone. Replace filename.txt with the file you want to delete. Always double-check the filename before running.

commands.title: Delete a folder and everything inside it
commands.description: Permanently deletes a folder and all its contents — all files and subfolders inside. There is no undo. The -r flag means recursive (everything inside). Be very careful with this command.

commands.title: Copy a file to another location
commands.description: Makes a copy of a file and puts it somewhere else. The original file stays untouched. You can copy to a folder (ending with /) or give the copy a new name.

commands.title: Move or rename a file
commands.description: Either moves a file to a new location or renames it, depending on what you specify. If you give a new name in the same folder, it renames. If you give a different folder path, it moves.

commands.title: Find a file anywhere on your computer
commands.description: Searches your home folder and all subfolders for a file matching the name you give. You can use wildcards like *.txt to find all text files. The search can take a moment on large drives.

commands.title: Search for text inside files
commands.description: Searches recursively through all files in a folder for lines containing your search text. Shows the filename and the matching line. Case-sensitive by default — add -i to ignore case.

commands.title: See how much space a folder is using
commands.description: Shows the total disk space used by a folder and everything inside it, in a human-readable format (MB, GB). Useful for finding what is taking up space on your drive.

commands.title: See how much free disk space you have
commands.description: Shows all your disk partitions, their total size, how much is used, and how much is free. The -h flag shows sizes in GB and MB instead of raw bytes.

commands.title: View the contents of a text file
commands.description: Prints the entire contents of a file directly in the terminal. Best for short files. For long files, use less which lets you scroll. Replace filename.txt with your file.

commands.title: Open a file with its default application
commands.description: Opens a file using whichever application is set as the default for that file type. Works like double-clicking a file in the file manager. Great for opening PDFs, images, or any document.

commands.title: Create a .zip archive of a folder
commands.description: Compresses a folder and all its contents into a single .zip file. The -r flag means recursive — it includes all subfolders. Anyone on any operating system can open a .zip file.

commands.title: Extract (unzip) a .zip file
commands.description: Extracts all files from a .zip archive into the current folder. The extracted files appear in a subfolder with the same name as the archive. Works with any standard .zip file.

commands.title: Create a compressed .tar.gz archive
commands.description: Packs a folder into a compressed .tar.gz file (also called a tarball). This format is common on Linux. The -c creates, -z compresses with gzip, -f specifies the output filename.

commands.title: Extract a .tar.gz archive
commands.description: Extracts all contents from a .tar.gz file into the current folder. The -x extracts, -z handles gzip compression, -f specifies the filename. Common for installing software from source.

commands.title: Update the list of available software
commands.description: Downloads the latest information about available packages from Ubuntu's servers. Does not install anything. Always run this before installing new software so you get the latest version.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo). Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Install all available software updates
commands.description: Updates all currently installed software to the latest versions. First updates the package list, then upgrades everything. The -y flag automatically answers yes to all prompts.
commands.command: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo). Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Install a program
commands.description: Downloads and installs a program by name. Replace program-name with the exact package name (e.g., vlc, git, htop). If you are not sure of the name, use the apt search command first.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo). Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Uninstall a program
commands.description: Removes an installed program from your system. This does not delete your personal files or settings related to that program — just removes the program itself.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo). Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Search for a program to install
commands.description: Searches the Ubuntu software repository for packages matching your keyword. Shows the package name and a short description. Use the exact package name with apt install afterwards.

commands.title: See all installed programs
commands.description: Lists every package currently installed on your system. There are usually hundreds. Pipe it through grep to search for something specific, for example: apt list --installed | grep python

commands.title: Install a Snap app
commands.description: Installs an app from the Snap store, which is an alternative to apt. Many popular apps like Spotify, VS Code, and Slack are available as Snaps. Replace app-name with the actual name.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo). Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Restart the computer
commands.description: Safely shuts down all running programs and restarts the computer. Always save your work before running this. The computer will go through a full shutdown and start back up.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo). Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Shut down the computer
commands.description: Safely saves everything and turns off the computer immediately. All running programs will be closed. Always save your open files before running this command.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo). Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Check how long the computer has been running
commands.description: Shows how long the computer has been on since its last restart, along with the current time and the average system load. Useful for tracking stability.

commands.title: See which version of Linux you have
commands.description: Shows your Linux distribution name and version number (for example, Ubuntu 22.04). Useful when you need to know which version you are running for installing software or getting support.

commands.title: See which programs are using the most RAM
commands.description: Lists the top 10 running processes sorted by memory usage, from highest to lowest. Shows the program name and how much RAM it is using as a percentage of total memory.

commands.title: See all running programs
commands.description: Lists every process currently running on your system, who started it, and what resources it is using. There will be many entries — most are system processes running in the background.

commands.title: Force close a program by name
commands.description: Immediately stops all instances of a program by its name. For example, killall firefox closes all Firefox windows. Use this when a program is frozen and will not close normally.

commands.title: Force close a program by process ID
commands.description: Stops a specific process using its numeric ID. First find the PID using ps aux | grep program-name, then use that number here. The -9 flag forces an immediate kill.

commands.title: See how much RAM is available and used
commands.description: Shows total RAM, how much is used, how much is free, and how much is used for buffers/cache. The -h flag shows the values in MB and GB for easy reading.

commands.title: Check if a program is installed and where it is
commands.description: Tells you whether a program is installed on your system and shows the full path to it. If nothing is returned, the program is not installed or not in your PATH.

commands.title: See your CPU information
commands.description: Displays detailed information about your processor: the model name, number of cores, speed (GHz), and architecture. Useful to know what hardware you have.

commands.title: See detailed memory information
commands.description: Shows very detailed RAM statistics from the Linux kernel, including total memory, free memory, swap usage, and various memory caches. More detailed than free -h.

commands.title: Run a Python script
commands.description: Executes a Python 3 script file. Replace script.py with the path to your Python file. Make sure you are in the right folder first, or use the full path to the script.

commands.title: Install a Python package
commands.description: Downloads and installs a Python package from PyPI (the Python Package Index). Replace package-name with the name of the package, for example: pip3 install requests or pip3 install numpy.

commands.title: List installed Python packages
commands.description: Shows all Python packages currently installed in your Python environment, along with their version numbers. Useful to check if a package is already installed.

commands.title: Start a simple local web server
commands.description: Starts a basic web server in your current folder on port 8000. You can then open a browser and go to http://localhost:8000 to see the files. Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

commands.title: Check which version of Python is installed
commands.description: Prints the Python 3 version number installed on your system. Useful to know which features are available and whether you need to update.

commands.title: Run a Node.js script
commands.description: Executes a JavaScript file using Node.js. Replace script.js with your file name. Node.js lets you run JavaScript code outside of a browser, useful for backend scripts and tools.

commands.title: Install a Node.js package
commands.description: Downloads and installs a Node.js package from npm (Node Package Manager). Replace package-name with the package you need. Installs it in the node_modules folder of your current project.

commands.title: Create a new Git repository
commands.description: Initialises a new Git repository in your current folder. This starts tracking changes to all files in the folder. Run this once when starting a new project.

commands.title: Download a project from GitHub
commands.description: Downloads a complete copy of a GitHub repository to your computer, including all files and the full history of changes. Replace the URL with the actual repository address.

commands.title: See what files changed in your Git project
commands.description: Shows which files have been modified, which are new, and which are staged (ready to commit). Run this often to keep track of your work before saving changes.

commands.title: Save your changes to Git (commit)
commands.description: Stages all changed files and saves them to the Git history with a message describing what you did. Replace 'My changes' with a short description of what you changed.

commands.title: Upload your changes to GitHub
commands.description: Sends your committed changes to the remote repository on GitHub. You need to have set up a remote first with git clone or git remote add. You may be asked for your GitHub credentials.

commands.title: Download the latest changes from GitHub
commands.description: Fetches the newest changes from the remote repository and merges them into your current branch. Run this before starting work to make sure you have the latest version.

commands.title: See the history of changes in Git
commands.description: Shows a compact list of all past commits, one per line, with the short ID and message. Newest commits appear at the top. Press Q to exit the log view.

commands.title: See which Git branch you are on
commands.description: Lists all branches in your repository and highlights the current one with an asterisk. Branches let you work on new features without affecting the main code.

commands.title: Check if Bluetooth is turned on
commands.description: Shows whether the Bluetooth service is running on your system. Look for 'active (running)' in the output to confirm it is on. If it is stopped, you can start it.

commands.title: Turn Bluetooth on
commands.description: Powers on your Bluetooth adapter so it can discover and connect to devices. After turning it on, use the scan command to find nearby devices.
commands.shell_only_reason: bluetoothctl is interactive. Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Turn Bluetooth off
commands.description: Powers off your Bluetooth adapter to save battery and prevent other devices from seeing your computer. Run bluetoothctl power on to turn it back on.
commands.shell_only_reason: bluetoothctl is interactive. Copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List paired Bluetooth devices
commands.description: Shows all Bluetooth devices that have been paired with your computer, along with their addresses. From this list you can see the device address needed to connect.

commands.title: Scan for nearby Bluetooth devices
commands.description: Starts scanning for Bluetooth devices around you. After a few seconds, you will see device names and addresses appearing. Press Ctrl+C to stop scanning.
commands.shell_only_reason: bluetoothctl is interactive — run in your terminal, then Ctrl+C to stop.

commands.title: List all connected USB devices
commands.description: Shows every USB device currently plugged into your computer, including mice, keyboards, USB drives, cameras, and hubs. Useful to confirm a device is being recognised.

commands.title: Show all storage drives and partitions
commands.description: Lists all block storage devices — hard drives, SSDs, USB drives, and their partitions. Shows the size of each one and where they are mounted in the filesystem.

commands.title: Check CPU and hardware temperatures
commands.description: Reads temperature sensors on your motherboard and CPU. Shows current temperatures in Celsius for each sensor. Useful for checking if your computer is overheating. May need: sudo apt install lm-sensors

commands.title: List PCI devices (graphics card, sound card, etc.)
commands.description: Shows all devices connected to your computer's PCI bus, including the graphics card, network card, and sound card. Useful for identifying hardware components.

commands.title: Check battery level and status
commands.description: Shows the current battery percentage, whether it is charging or discharging, and the estimated time remaining. Works on laptops. The exact output depends on your hardware.

commands.title: Show your username
commands.description: Prints the username you are currently logged in as. Useful in scripts or when you are not sure which user account you are using, especially after switching users.

commands.title: See who is logged into the computer
commands.description: Shows all users currently logged into the system, which terminal they are on, and when they logged in. On a single-user desktop, this usually shows just you.

commands.title: Show your user ID and group memberships
commands.description: Displays your numeric user ID (UID), group ID (GID), and all the groups you belong to. Groups determine what resources and commands you have access to on the system.

commands.title: Change your login password
commands.description: Starts an interactive process to change your account password. You will be asked for your current password first, then the new one twice. Your new password must be reasonably strong.
commands.shell_only_reason: passwd is interactive and needs a live terminal to type your password.

commands.title: Count the number of lines in a file
commands.description: Counts and prints the number of lines in a text file. Useful for quickly knowing how long a file is without opening it. Works well combined with other commands.

commands.title: Show the first lines of a file
commands.description: Displays the first 20 lines of a file. Useful for getting a quick look at the beginning of a large file without loading the whole thing. Change 20 to any number.

commands.title: Show the last lines of a file
commands.description: Displays the last 20 lines of a file. Change 20 to see more or fewer lines. The -f flag makes it keep showing new lines as they are added — great for watching log files live.

commands.title: Watch a log file update in real time
commands.description: Keeps the file open and prints new lines as they are written. Perfect for monitoring log files while troubleshooting. Press Ctrl+C to stop watching.

commands.title: Sort the lines of a file alphabetically
commands.description: Reads a file and prints all its lines sorted in alphabetical order. Does not change the original file — just shows the sorted output on screen. Add > sorted.txt to save the result.

commands.title: Find and replace text inside a file
commands.description: Replaces every occurrence of 'old text' with 'new text' inside a file. The -i flag edits the file directly. The g at the end means replace all occurrences, not just the first one.

commands.title: Connect to a remote server
commands.description: Opens a secure SSH connection to a remote server. Replace user with your username on the server and server.com with the server address or IP. You will be asked for the server password.
commands.shell_only_reason: SSH opens an interactive session — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Connect to a server on a specific port
commands.description: Connects to a server using a non-standard SSH port. The default SSH port is 22, but many servers use a different one (like 2222) for security reasons. Replace 2222 with the actual port number.
commands.shell_only_reason: SSH opens an interactive session — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Connect to a server using an SSH key file
commands.description: Connects to a server using a private key file instead of a password. The -i flag specifies the key file. This is more secure and is required by cloud providers like AWS and DigitalOcean.
commands.shell_only_reason: SSH opens an interactive session — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Run a single command on a remote server
commands.description: Connects to a server, runs one command, shows its output, then disconnects immediately. You do not need to log in manually. Replace the quoted command with whatever you want to run.

commands.title: Create a new SSH key pair
commands.description: Generates a secure SSH key pair — a private key that stays on your computer and a public key that goes on servers. The -t ed25519 uses the strongest modern algorithm.

commands.title: Add your SSH key to a server so you can log in without a password
commands.description: Copies your public SSH key to a remote server and adds it to the list of authorised keys. After this, you can SSH into that server without typing a password every time.

commands.title: Upload a file to a remote server
commands.description: Securely copies a file from your computer to a folder on a remote server. SCP uses SSH so the transfer is encrypted. Replace the path after the colon with where you want the file to land.

commands.title: Download a file from a remote server
commands.description: Securely copies a file from a remote server to your current folder. The dot at the end means 'here'. Replace the server path with the full path to the file on the server.

commands.title: Copy an entire folder to a remote server
commands.description: Uploads a complete folder including all its subfolders to a remote server. The -r flag means recursive. Useful for deploying a website or uploading a project.

commands.title: Sync a local folder with a remote server (only copies what changed)
commands.description: Like scp but smarter — it only transfers files that have changed since the last sync. Much faster for repeated backups or deployments. The -avz flags mean: preserve all attributes, show progress, compress the data.

commands.title: Download and sync a folder from a remote server
commands.description: Downloads a folder from a server to your computer, only transferring files that have changed. The direction is reversed — the server path comes first. Great for keeping a local backup of server data.

commands.title: Create an SSH tunnel to access a remote port locally
commands.description: Forwards a port from a remote server to your own computer. For example, this lets you access a database running on the server as if it were running locally. Open your browser to http://localhost:8080 after running.
commands.shell_only_reason: SSH tunnels need an interactive session — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Connect to a server and prevent automatic disconnection
commands.description: Opens an SSH connection that sends a heartbeat every 60 seconds to prevent the server from timing out and dropping you. Useful for long-running sessions or slow networks.
commands.shell_only_reason: SSH opens an interactive session — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: See the firewall status and all its rules
commands.description: Shows whether the firewall (UFW) is active and lists every rule — which ports are open and which are blocked. Always check this before and after changing firewall rules.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo) — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Open a port in the firewall
commands.description: Allows incoming connections on a specific port. For example: allow 22 opens SSH, allow 80 opens HTTP, allow 443 opens HTTPS. Replace 22 with the port number you need.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo) — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Turn the firewall on
commands.description: Enables the UFW firewall so it starts blocking unwanted connections. Before enabling on a remote server, make sure SSH (port 22) is allowed, or you will lock yourself out.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo) — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Test if a specific port is open on a server
commands.description: Tests whether a port on a server accepts connections. Useful for checking if a firewall is blocking something or if a service is listening. If it connects, the port is open.

commands.title: Trace the network path to a server hop by hop
commands.description: Shows every router your data passes through on the way to a destination, with the time each hop takes. Useful for finding where a slow or broken connection is occurring.

commands.title: Look up a domain name to find its IP address
commands.description: Asks your DNS server to translate a domain name into its IP address. Also shows which DNS server answered. Useful for checking if a domain resolves correctly.

commands.title: Check if a service is running on the server
commands.description: Shows the current status of a service — whether it is running, stopped, or crashed — and the last few lines of its log. Replace service-name with nginx, apache2, mysql, postgresql, etc.

commands.title: Start a stopped service
commands.description: Starts a service that is currently stopped. Replace service-name with the actual name, for example: nginx, apache2, mysql, postgresql, redis. Requires administrator rights.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo) — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Restart a service (apply config changes)
commands.description: Stops and then starts a service again. Use this after changing a service's configuration file to apply the new settings. Works with nginx, apache2, mysql, and any systemd service.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo) — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Make a service start automatically when the server boots
commands.description: Registers a service to start automatically every time the computer or server boots up. Without this, you would have to manually start the service after every reboot.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires administrator password (sudo) — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: View system and service error logs
commands.description: Opens the system journal which contains logs from the operating system and all services. The -xe flags jump to the most recent entries and show extra context. Press Q to exit.

commands.title: Watch server logs live as they come in
commands.description: Follows a log file and prints each new line as it is written. Essential for monitoring a web server, watching for errors, or debugging a running service. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

commands.title: Scan a host for open ports
commands.description: Scans the 1000 most common ports on a target to see which are open. Replace 192.168.1.1 with the IP or hostname you want to scan. Only scan machines you own or have permission to test.

commands.title: Scan all devices on your local network
commands.description: Scans the entire 192.168.1.0/24 subnet (256 addresses) to discover all active hosts and their open ports. Useful for auditing your own home or office network.

commands.title: Detect the operating system of a remote host
commands.description: Tries to identify the operating system and version running on a remote machine by analysing network responses. Requires root/sudo privileges for accurate results.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo for OS detection — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Scan for common vulnerabilities with nmap scripts
commands.description: Runs nmap's built-in vulnerability detection scripts against a target. These scripts check for well-known security issues. Only use on systems you own or are authorised to test.

commands.title: Discover which hosts are alive on a network
commands.description: Quickly pings all addresses in a subnet to find which machines are online, without scanning ports. Much faster than a full scan. Great for getting a map of your network.

commands.title: Look up all DNS records for a domain
commands.description: Queries DNS servers for all record types associated with a domain — A, MX, NS, TXT, and more. More detailed than nslookup. Replace google.com with any domain you want to inspect.

commands.title: Trace DNS resolution from root servers
commands.description: Follows the entire DNS resolution chain from root nameservers down to the authoritative server for a domain. Useful for diagnosing DNS hijacking or misconfiguration.

commands.title: Look up registration info for a domain or IP
commands.description: Queries the WHOIS database to find who registered a domain, when it expires, and which nameservers it uses. Works for domains and IP addresses. Useful for threat intelligence.

commands.title: Capture all live network traffic
commands.description: Captures packets on your primary network interface and prints them to the screen. Press Ctrl+C to stop. Requires sudo. Output can be very fast — pipe to a file or use filters.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Capture traffic on a specific port
commands.description: Captures and displays only the packets going to or from a specific port. Replace 80 with any port number. Great for debugging HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), SSH (22), or any service.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Save captured network traffic to a file
commands.description: Captures all packets and writes them to a .pcap file that you can later open in Wireshark for detailed analysis. Replace eth0 with your interface name (from ip link show).
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: View an SSL certificate for a website
commands.description: Connects to a website and displays its SSL/TLS certificate details — who issued it, when it expires, and what domains it covers. Replace google.com with any domain to inspect.
commands.command: echo | openssl s_client -connect google.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text

commands.title: Check when an SSL certificate expires
commands.description: Quickly shows only the start and expiry dates of a site's SSL certificate. Useful for monitoring whether certificates are about to expire. Replace the domain with your target.
commands.command: echo | openssl s_client -connect google.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

commands.title: Generate a new private key and self-signed certificate
commands.description: Creates a 2048-bit RSA private key and a self-signed SSL certificate valid for 365 days. Useful for testing HTTPS locally. The key.pem is private — keep it secret.

commands.title: Create a SHA-256 hash of a file
commands.description: Calculates the SHA-256 cryptographic hash (fingerprint) of a file. Use this to verify that a downloaded file has not been tampered with by comparing its hash with the official one.

commands.title: Generate a new GPG encryption key pair
commands.description: Starts the interactive process to create a GPG key pair — a public key to share and a private key to keep secret. Used to encrypt files and sign emails or commits.
commands.shell_only_reason: gpg --gen-key is interactive — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List all GPG keys in your keyring
commands.description: Shows all GPG keys stored on your system — both public keys from other people and your own key pairs. Displays key IDs, email addresses, and expiry dates.

commands.title: Encrypt a file with GPG for a recipient
commands.description: Encrypts a file so that only the person with the matching private key can read it. Replace recipient@email.com with their email (their public key must be in your keyring first).

commands.title: Decrypt a GPG-encrypted file
commands.description: Decrypts a .gpg file that was encrypted for you. GPG will ask for your private key passphrase. The decrypted content is saved to file.txt (remove -o to print to screen).

commands.title: List all active firewall rules (iptables)
commands.description: Displays all current iptables firewall rules in a numbered, easy-to-read format. Shows which connections are accepted, dropped, or rejected. Requires sudo.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Block all traffic from a specific IP address
commands.description: Adds a rule to immediately drop all incoming packets from an IP address. Useful for blocking an attacker or unwanted source. Replace the IP with the address you want to block.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo and affects your network — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Check fail2ban protection status
commands.description: Shows which fail2ban jails are active. Fail2ban automatically bans IPs that have too many failed login attempts. Run this to confirm it is protecting services like SSH and nginx.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: See who fail2ban has banned from SSH
commands.description: Shows the fail2ban SSH jail details: how many failures are allowed, the ban time, and a list of currently banned IP addresses. Useful for monitoring brute-force attempts.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Run a full system security audit with Lynis
commands.description: Lynis scans your entire system for security misconfigurations, outdated software, missing patches, and hardening opportunities. Generates a score and suggestions. May need: sudo apt install lynis
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo and takes several minutes — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Scan for rootkits and backdoors
commands.description: Rootkit Hunter scans your system for known rootkits, backdoors, and suspicious files that an attacker may have planted. Run periodically as a health check. May need: sudo apt install rkhunter
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Check for rootkits with chkrootkit
commands.description: Another rootkit scanner that checks for signs of compromise including suspicious processes, hidden files, and known rootkit signatures. May need: sudo apt install chkrootkit
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Scan a directory for viruses with ClamAV
commands.description: Scans a folder (here your home directory) for known viruses and malware. Reports infected files but does not delete them unless you add --remove. May need: sudo apt install clamav

commands.title: Find files with SUID bit set (potential privilege escalation)
commands.description: Lists all executable files with the SUID bit set — these run as the file owner (often root) regardless of who launches them. Attackers look for these to escalate privileges. Review any unexpected results.

commands.title: Find world-writable files and directories
commands.description: Lists files and directories that anyone on the system can write to. These are potential security risks — attackers can plant malicious files in world-writable locations.

commands.title: Show all established network connections
commands.description: Lists only the connections that are currently active and exchanging data, with the remote address and port. Useful for spotting unexpected outgoing connections that could indicate a compromise.

commands.title: Show all listening ports and active connections
commands.description: Displays all open ports and established connections along with the process that opened them. Use this to audit what services are exposed and spot rogue processes making network calls.

commands.title: See recent login history
commands.description: Shows a list of all recent successful logins — username, terminal, source IP (for SSH), and date/time. Review this to spot any unauthorised access to your system.

commands.title: See failed login attempts
commands.description: Shows recent failed login attempts including the username tried and source IP address. A high number of failures from one IP usually indicates a brute-force attack. Requires sudo.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Watch the authentication log for suspicious logins
commands.description: Shows the last 50 lines of the authentication log, which records every login attempt, sudo use, and SSH connection. Useful for spotting attacks in real time.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Inspect HTTP security headers of a website
commands.description: Fetches just the HTTP response headers from a URL without downloading the page body. Look for security headers like Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options, and Content-Security-Policy.

commands.title: Scan a web server for security vulnerabilities
commands.description: Nikto is a web server scanner that checks for dangerous files, outdated software, and common misconfigurations. Only scan servers you own or have permission to test. May need: sudo apt install nikto

commands.title: Crack password hashes with John the Ripper
commands.description: John the Ripper tries to recover passwords from hash files. Only use this on your own systems — for example, to test password strength or recover a forgotten hash. Requires: sudo apt install john
commands.shell_only_reason: Use only on hashes you own or are authorised to test — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Test SSH login with a password list (authorised testing only)
commands.description: Hydra tries to log into an SSH server using a list of passwords. Use ONLY on your own systems or in authorised penetration tests. Illegal use is a criminal offence. Requires: sudo apt install hydra
commands.shell_only_reason: Use ONLY on systems you own or are authorised to test — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: GPU-accelerated password hash cracking (authorised use only)
commands.description: Hashcat uses your GPU to crack password hashes at high speed. Replace 0 with the hash type (0=MD5, 100=SHA1, 1800=SHA-512). Use ONLY on hashes you own or are authorised to test.
commands.shell_only_reason: Use ONLY on hashes you own or are authorised to test — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Check AppArmor security profiles
commands.description: Shows the status of AppArmor — Linux's mandatory access control system. Lists which applications have security profiles enforced, which are in complain mode, and which are unconfined.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List active audit rules (auditd)
commands.description: Shows all rules currently loaded into the Linux audit daemon (auditd). Audit rules track system calls, file access, and user actions. Useful for compliance and intrusion detection.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Block a port in the firewall (UFW)
commands.description: Adds a rule to deny all incoming connections on a specific port. Replace 23 with the port you want to block. For example, blocking port 23 disables Telnet access.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Remove a firewall rule (UFW)
commands.description: Deletes a specific UFW rule. Run 'sudo ufw status numbered' first to see rule numbers, then replace N with the number of the rule you want to remove.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Check password expiry info for your account
commands.description: Shows the password ageing and expiry settings for your user account — when the password was last changed, when it expires, and how many days before expiry you get a warning.

commands.title: Check default file permission mask
commands.description: Displays the current umask — the default permission mask applied to all newly created files and directories. A umask of 022 means new files are readable by everyone; 077 makes them private.

commands.title: List processes with open network connections
commands.description: Shows every process that currently has an open network connection, along with the remote address and port. Helps identify unexpected programs phoning home.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo for full results — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Extract readable text from a binary file
commands.description: Prints all human-readable strings found inside a binary file. Useful for quickly inspecting a suspicious file or executable to see if it contains IP addresses, URLs, or other clues.

commands.title: Search for a package by name or description
commands.description: Searches the package database for anything matching your keyword — package names and descriptions. Useful when you know what you want to install but not the exact package name.

commands.title: Show details about a package
commands.description: Displays full information about a package: version, size, dependencies, and description. Run this before installing to know what you are getting.

commands.title: List all installed packages
commands.description: Shows every package currently installed on your system with its version. Pipe to grep to filter: dpkg -l | grep python lists all Python-related packages.

commands.title: Remove a package (keep config files)
commands.description: Uninstalls a package but keeps its configuration files. Useful if you plan to reinstall later and want to keep your settings. Use purge to remove config files too.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Completely remove a package and its config files
commands.description: Uninstalls a package and deletes all its configuration files. Use this for a clean removal when you no longer want any trace of the software.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Remove packages that are no longer needed
commands.description: Removes packages that were installed as dependencies but are no longer needed by anything. Run this after removing software to clean up orphaned packages.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List all installed Snap packages
commands.description: Shows all Snap apps installed on your system with their version and channel. Snap packages are self-contained and update automatically.

commands.title: Install a Snap package
commands.description: Installs an application from the Snap store. Snap packages work across many Linux distributions. Browse available apps at snapcraft.io.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Remove a Snap package
commands.description: Uninstalls a Snap application. Unlike apt, Snap keeps a revision of the package for a short time so you can roll back.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List all installed Flatpak apps
commands.description: Shows all Flatpak applications installed on your system. Flatpak apps are sandboxed and work across distributions.

commands.title: Install a Flatpak application
commands.description: Installs an app from Flathub, the main Flatpak repository. Most popular Linux apps are available here. Browse at flathub.org.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires interactive confirmation — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List all installed Python packages
commands.description: Shows every Python package installed in the current environment with its version. Use pip3 list --outdated to see which ones have updates available.

commands.title: Show outdated Python packages
commands.description: Lists all installed Python packages that have a newer version available. Shows the current version and the latest version side by side.

commands.title: Upgrade a Python package to the latest version
commands.description: Updates a specific Python package to its latest version. Replace package-name with the actual package. Use pip3 install --upgrade pip to update pip itself.

commands.title: List running Docker containers
commands.description: Shows all containers that are currently running, with their ID, image, status, and exposed ports. Add -a to also see stopped containers.

commands.title: List all Docker containers including stopped ones
commands.description: Shows every container on your system — running, stopped, and exited — with their status and when they last ran.

commands.title: List all Docker images
commands.description: Shows all Docker images downloaded on your system, with their name, tag, size, and creation date. Images are the blueprints containers are built from.

commands.title: Run a Docker container
commands.description: Starts a new container from an image. -d runs it in the background (detached). -p 8080:80 maps port 8080 on your machine to port 80 in the container. Replace nginx with any image name.

commands.title: Run a command inside a running container
commands.description: Opens a bash shell inside a running container so you can explore it, check files, or debug. Replace container-id with the ID or name from docker ps.

commands.title: View logs from a Docker container
commands.description: Shows the output (stdout and stderr) from a container. Add -f to follow logs in real time, like tail -f. Add --tail 100 to only show the last 100 lines.

commands.title: Stop a running Docker container
commands.description: Gracefully stops a running container by sending it a SIGTERM signal and giving it 10 seconds to shut down cleanly before forcing it to stop.

commands.title: Remove a stopped Docker container
commands.description: Deletes a stopped container permanently. The image it was built from is kept. Use docker rm -f to force-remove a running container.

commands.title: Remove a Docker image
commands.description: Deletes a Docker image from your local storage. All containers using it must be stopped and removed first. Frees up disk space.

commands.title: Download a Docker image
commands.description: Downloads an image from Docker Hub (or another registry) to your local machine. Run this before docker run if you want to pre-download an image.

commands.title: Build a Docker image from a Dockerfile
commands.description: Builds a new image from a Dockerfile in the current directory. The -t flag gives it a name and tag. Replace myapp:1.0 with your chosen name.

commands.title: Start all services defined in docker-compose.yml
commands.description: Reads docker-compose.yml and starts all defined services. -d runs them in the background. Use this to bring up a full multi-container application with one command.

commands.title: Stop and remove all Docker Compose services
commands.description: Stops all containers defined in docker-compose.yml and removes them. Add --volumes to also delete associated data volumes. The images are kept.

commands.title: Remove all unused Docker resources
commands.description: Deletes all stopped containers, unused images, and unused networks in one go. A safe way to free up disk space. Add --volumes to also remove unused volumes.

commands.title: Show disk space usage on all drives
commands.description: Displays how much disk space is used and available on each mounted filesystem in a human-readable format (GB, MB). Run this to quickly see if any drive is nearly full.

commands.title: Show how much space a folder is using
commands.description: Calculates the total size of a directory and all its contents. -h shows sizes in human-readable format. -s shows only the total, not each subfolder. Change the path to any directory.

commands.title: Find the largest folders in a directory
commands.description: Lists the 10 biggest subdirectories under the current directory, sorted by size. Useful for tracking down what is filling up your disk.

commands.title: Show all drives and their partitions
commands.description: Lists all block devices (hard drives, SSDs, USB drives, NVMe) with their partitions, sizes, types, and mount points in a tree layout.

commands.title: Show all currently mounted filesystems
commands.description: Lists every filesystem currently mounted on your system, including USB drives, network mounts, and virtual filesystems. Shows the device, mount point, and type.

commands.title: Mount a USB drive manually
commands.description: Mounts a partition (e.g. /dev/sdb1) to a folder so you can access its files. Create the folder first with mkdir -p /mnt/usb. Use lsblk to find the device name.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Safely unmount a drive before removing it
commands.description: Unmounts a drive so it is safe to physically remove. Always unmount USB drives before unplugging them to avoid data corruption.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Interactive disk usage explorer (ncdu)
commands.description: Opens a full-screen interactive browser for exploring disk usage. Navigate with arrow keys, press d to delete a folder, q to quit. Much easier than du. May need: sudo apt install ncdu

commands.title: Optimise SSD performance (TRIM)
commands.description: Sends TRIM commands to your SSD to mark deleted blocks as available, improving write performance. Run this periodically if you have an SSD. Most modern systems do this automatically weekly.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Check if your hard drive is healthy
commands.description: Runs a SMART health check on your primary hard drive and prints a summary. Look for 'PASSED' in the output. May need: sudo apt install smartmontools
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Run a command with lower CPU priority
commands.description: Starts a program with a lower priority (niceness 10) so it does not slow down other work. Niceness ranges from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). Use for long background tasks like backups or video encoding.

commands.title: Change the priority of a running process
commands.description: Adjusts the CPU priority of an already-running process. Replace 1234 with the PID from ps or top. Higher niceness = lower priority. Useful for taming runaway processes.

commands.title: Run a command with lower disk I/O priority
commands.description: Starts a process with best-effort I/O class at priority 7 (lowest). Prevents disk-heavy tasks like backups from making everything else sluggish.

commands.title: Check how aggressively Linux uses swap
commands.description: Reads the current swappiness value. 60 is the default — Linux starts swapping when RAM usage crosses ~40%. Lower values (10-20) make Linux prefer keeping things in RAM, which is better for SSDs.

commands.title: Reduce swap usage to improve performance
commands.description: Sets swappiness to 10 so Linux avoids using swap unless RAM is very low. Good for systems with SSDs. This change is temporary — add it to /etc/sysctl.conf to make it permanent.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List all kernel parameters
commands.description: Prints every tunable kernel parameter and its current value. Pipe to grep to find specific ones: sysctl -a | grep net.ipv4 shows network settings.

commands.title: Show resource limits for the current shell
commands.description: Displays all resource limits set for the current user session — maximum file size, number of open files, stack size, and more. These prevent runaway processes from consuming all resources.

commands.title: Show virtual memory and CPU statistics
commands.description: Displays a snapshot of memory usage, swap, I/O, and CPU activity. The columns show processes, memory, swap, I/O, system calls, and CPU percentages. Good for a quick system overview.

commands.title: Show recent kernel messages
commands.description: Prints the most recent messages from the kernel ring buffer — hardware events, driver errors, USB connections, and boot messages. Use this to diagnose hardware problems.

commands.title: Show only kernel errors and warnings
commands.description: Filters kernel messages to show only errors and warnings. A clean system should show very few entries here. Lots of errors may indicate hardware or driver problems.

commands.title: Show all log messages from the current boot
commands.description: Displays every system log entry since the last reboot. Use -b -1 to see logs from the previous boot. Useful for diagnosing startup problems.

commands.title: Show logs for a specific service
commands.description: Displays all log entries from a particular service. Replace nginx with the service name you want to investigate. Add -f to follow logs in real time.

commands.title: Trace all system calls made by a command
commands.description: Shows every system call a program makes — file opens, network connections, memory allocations. Invaluable for debugging why a command fails. Output can be very verbose.

commands.title: Show which libraries a program depends on
commands.description: Lists all shared libraries that a binary needs to run. Use this to diagnose 'library not found' errors or to understand what a program depends on.

commands.title: Trace library calls made by a program
commands.description: Like strace but shows calls to shared library functions (libc, etc.) rather than raw system calls. Useful for debugging programs that use external libraries.

commands.title: List recent application crash dumps
commands.description: Shows all recorded application crashes (core dumps) captured by systemd-coredump. Useful for finding out what crashed and when.

commands.title: Show your scheduled cron jobs
commands.description: Lists all cron jobs scheduled for the current user. Each line shows when the job runs (minute, hour, day, month, weekday) followed by the command.

commands.title: Edit your cron jobs
commands.description: Opens the cron job file in your default editor. Each line is: minute hour day month weekday command. Example: 0 2 * * * means 'every day at 2am'. Changes take effect immediately on save.
commands.shell_only_reason: crontab -e is interactive — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Check what a cron expression means
commands.description: Shows all currently loaded cron jobs across all users. Use this to audit what is scheduled on the system. Requires root to see other users' crons.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List all systemd timer units
commands.description: Shows all systemd timers — the modern alternative to cron. Displays when each timer last ran and when it will run next. Much more reliable than cron for system tasks.

commands.title: Run a command once at a specific time
commands.description: Schedules a one-time command to run at a specific time. The 'at' prompt waits for your command — type it and press Ctrl+D to confirm. May need: sudo apt install at
commands.shell_only_reason: at is interactive — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: List pending scheduled 'at' jobs
commands.description: Shows all one-time jobs that are scheduled with the 'at' command but have not run yet. Use atrm JOB_NUMBER to cancel one.

commands.title: Show the network routing table
commands.description: Displays all IP routes — how your system decides where to send network packets. Shows your default gateway and any specific routes for subnets.

commands.title: Show all network interfaces and their IP addresses
commands.description: Lists every network interface (ethernet, WiFi, loopback, VPN) with its current IP address, MAC address, and state. More powerful than the deprecated ifconfig.

commands.title: Show the ARP table (local network devices)
commands.description: Lists all devices your computer has recently communicated with on the local network, with their IP and MAC addresses. Useful for finding devices on your network.

commands.title: Trace network route with live statistics
commands.description: Combines traceroute and ping in one tool. Shows every hop to a destination with live packet loss and latency statistics. Much more useful than traceroute alone. May need: sudo apt install mtr

commands.title: Show live network bandwidth usage by connection
commands.description: Displays real-time bandwidth usage for each active network connection — which hosts are transferring data and how fast. Press q to quit. May need: sudo apt install iftop
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Show live bandwidth usage by process
commands.description: Shows which processes are using the most network bandwidth in real time, with upload and download speeds per process. Like top but for network. May need: sudo apt install nethogs
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: Show which process is using a specific port
commands.description: Finds which process is listening on a given port. Replace 8080 with your port number. Useful when a port is already in use and you need to know what is using it.

commands.title: Make an API request and format the JSON response
commands.description: Sends a GET request to a URL and pipes the response through jq to pretty-print it with colours and formatting. Replace the URL with your API endpoint. May need: sudo apt install jq

commands.title: Print specific columns from a file or output
commands.description: awk is a powerful text processor. This prints the 1st and 3rd columns from a file (columns are separated by spaces). Change $1 $3 to any column numbers you need.

commands.title: Sum a column of numbers with awk
commands.description: Adds up all numbers in the first column of a file and prints the total. Change $1 to the column number you want to sum. Works great on the output of df, ps, or CSV files.

commands.title: Extract specific fields from a delimited file
commands.description: Cuts out specific fields from a file based on a delimiter. -d',' uses comma as the delimiter, -f1,3 extracts fields 1 and 3. Perfect for CSV files.

commands.title: Replace or delete characters in text
commands.description: Translates (replaces) characters in a stream. This example converts all lowercase letters to uppercase. tr -d '\n' removes all newlines. tr -s ' ' squeezes multiple spaces to one.

commands.title: Merge lines from two files side by side
commands.description: Combines two files column by column, separated by a tab. If file1 has names and file2 has ages, the output has both on each line. Use -d',' for CSV output.

commands.title: Compare two files and show differences
commands.description: Shows what is different between two files. Lines starting with < are only in the first file, > are only in the second. Use diff -u for a unified format (like a git diff).

commands.title: Apply a patch file to update code
commands.description: Applies changes from a .patch file (produced by diff) to update a file or directory. The -p1 flag strips the leading directory from paths in the patch. Used for applying patches from mailing lists or bug reports.

commands.title: Query and filter JSON data
commands.description: jq is a command-line JSON processor. The dot extracts the entire document. Use .key to get a field, .array[] to iterate, and .[] | select(.active==true) to filter. May need: sudo apt install jq

commands.title: Search for text in all files in a directory
commands.description: Searches every file in a directory and its subdirectories for a pattern. -r is recursive, -n shows line numbers, -i makes it case-insensitive. Great for searching codebases.

commands.title: Run a command on each result from a search
commands.description: Takes output from one command and runs another command for each item. This example finds all .log files and deletes them. The -I{} puts each result in place of {}. Very powerful for bulk operations.

commands.title: Create a compressed archive (.tar.gz)
commands.description: Compresses a directory into a single .tar.gz file. -c creates, -z uses gzip compression, -v shows progress, -f sets the output filename. This is the most common archive format on Linux.

commands.title: Extract a .tar.gz archive
commands.description: Extracts all files from a .tar.gz archive into the current directory. -x extracts, -z handles gzip, -v shows filenames as they are extracted, -f specifies the file.

commands.title: List contents of an archive without extracting
commands.description: Shows all files inside a .tar.gz archive without actually extracting anything. Useful to inspect an archive before unpacking it. Replace .gz with nothing for uncompressed tar files.

commands.title: Create a ZIP archive
commands.description: Creates a ZIP file from a directory. The -r flag makes it recursive (includes all subdirectories). ZIP is compatible with Windows and Mac without extra tools.

commands.title: Create a password-protected ZIP archive
commands.description: Creates an encrypted ZIP file requiring a password to open. You will be prompted to enter and confirm the password. Note: ZIP encryption is not very strong — use GPG for sensitive data.

commands.title: Extract a ZIP archive
commands.description: Extracts all files from a ZIP archive into the current directory. Use -d /path/to/folder to extract to a specific location.

commands.title: Compress a single file with gzip
commands.description: Compresses a file using gzip. The original file is replaced by file.gz. Use gunzip file.gz to decompress, or gzip -k file to keep the original.

commands.title: Create a 7z archive (best compression)
commands.description: Creates a 7z archive with high compression. 7z usually achieves better compression than zip or gzip. May need: sudo apt install p7zip-full

commands.title: Search your command history
commands.description: Searches through all previously typed commands for a keyword and shows matches with their history numbers. Press Ctrl+R in the terminal for an interactive history search.

commands.title: Re-run a command from history by number
commands.description: Runs a specific command from your history by its number. Use history to see numbers. The ! prefix tells bash to look up the history. !-1 runs the last command (same as pressing Up then Enter).

commands.title: List all active shell aliases
commands.description: Shows all aliases defined in your current shell session and loaded from your .bashrc or .zshrc. Aliases are shortcuts for longer commands.

commands.title: Create a command shortcut (alias)
commands.description: Creates a temporary alias for the current session. For example, alias ll='ls -la' makes ll show a detailed file list. To make it permanent, add this line to your ~/.bashrc file.

commands.title: Show all environment variables
commands.description: Prints all environment variables set in the current shell session — paths, user info, locale settings, and any custom variables you have defined.

commands.title: Set an environment variable
commands.description: Sets an environment variable that is visible to all child processes started from this shell. To make it permanent, add it to ~/.bashrc (for bash) or ~/.zshrc (for zsh).

commands.title: Reload shell config without restarting
commands.description: Reloads your .bashrc file so new aliases, functions, and environment variables take effect immediately without opening a new terminal. Use source ~/.zshrc for zsh.

commands.title: Find where a command is installed
commands.description: Shows the full path to an executable. Useful for confirming which version of a program will run (e.g. if you have multiple Python versions installed).

commands.title: Check if a command is a builtin, alias, or file

commands.title: Open a file or URL with the default application

commands.title: Make a file executable
commands.description: Adds execute permission to a file so you can run it as a script or program. +x adds execute permission for everyone. Use ./filename to run it.

commands.title: Make a file readable only by you
commands.description: Sets permissions to 600 — only the owner can read and write, nobody else can see or execute it. Use this for private keys, config files with passwords, and sensitive data.

commands.title: Set standard web file permissions (644 / 755)
commands.description: Sets permissions to 644 for files (owner can read/write, others can read) and 755 for directories (owner full access, others can read and enter). The standard setup for web server files.
commands.command: find /var/www -type f -exec chmod 644 {} \; && find /var/www -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;

commands.title: Change who owns a file
commands.description: Changes the owner of a file. Replace username with the user who should own it. Use username:groupname to also change the group. Requires sudo if you do not own the file.

commands.title: Change ownership of a whole folder
commands.description: Changes the owner of a directory and everything inside it. -R is recursive. Use this to fix ownership problems, for example after copying files as root.
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires sudo — copy and run in your terminal.

commands.title: View extended file permissions (ACL)
commands.description: Shows the full Access Control List for a file, including permissions for specific users and groups beyond the standard owner/group/other model. May need: sudo apt install acl

commands.title: Grant a specific user access to a file (ACL)
commands.description: Adds an extended permission allowing a specific user to read and write a file without changing the standard permissions. More flexible than chmod. May need: sudo apt install acl

commands.title: Create a Python virtual environment
commands.description: Creates an isolated Python environment in a folder called venv. Activate it with 'source venv/bin/activate'. Packages installed there won't affect the rest of your system.

commands.title: Activate a Python virtual environment
commands.description: Activates the virtual environment in the current folder. Your prompt changes to show (venv). Now pip install goes into the venv, not the system. Use 'deactivate' to exit.

commands.title: Install Node.js dependencies from package.json
commands.description: Reads package.json and installs all listed dependencies into node_modules. Always run this after cloning a Node.js project before trying to run it.

commands.title: Run a script defined in package.json
commands.description: Runs a script from the scripts section of package.json. Common scripts are start, build, test, and dev. Replace start with whichever script you need.

commands.title: Run a Node.js package without installing it

commands.title: Temporarily save uncommitted changes
commands.description: Saves your current uncommitted changes to a stack and reverts the working directory to the last commit. Use git stash pop to restore them. Useful when you need to switch branches but are not ready to commit.

commands.title: Restore stashed changes
commands.description: Applies the most recently stashed changes back to your working directory and removes them from the stash. Use git stash list to see all stashes and git stash apply stash@{1} for a specific one.

commands.title: Rebase your branch onto another branch
commands.description: Replays your branch's commits on top of another branch (usually main). Creates a cleaner linear history than merging. Warning: do not rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote.

commands.title: Apply a specific commit to your current branch
commands.description: Copies a single commit from anywhere in the git history and applies it to your current branch. Useful for backporting a bug fix to an older release branch.

commands.title: See what you have staged before committing
commands.description: Shows the exact changes that are staged (added with git add) and will be included in the next commit. Review this before committing to make sure you are committing the right things.

commands.title: Unstage a file without losing changes
commands.description: Removes a file from the staging area without discarding the changes. The file goes back to modified/untracked status. Use git checkout -- filename to discard changes entirely.

commands.description: Creates a new Python project with proper structure and a pyproject.toml. Poetry manages dependencies and virtual environments automatically. May need: pip install poetry

commands.title: Create a custom AI model (Modelfile)

cat > Modelfile << 'EOF'
FROM llama3
SYSTEM "You are a helpful Linux expert. Be concise and practical."
PARAMETER temperature 0.7
PARAMETER num_ctx 4096
EOF
commands.shell_only_reason: Edit the SYSTEM prompt to set your AI's personality, then run in terminal.

commands.title: Build model from Modelfile
