commands.description: Starts the Open WebUI server after pip installation. Opens a ChatGPT-like interface for your local Ollama models at http://localhost:8080.

commands.title: Install Fabric (AI pattern tool)
commands.description: Installs Fabric by Daniel Miessler — a tool for augmenting humans with AI using reusable 'patterns' (prompts). Pipe any text through AI patterns like 'summarise', 'extract wisdom', 'write essay', etc.

commands.title: Set up Fabric with API keys
commands.description: Runs Fabric's initial setup to configure your AI provider API keys and default model. Run this once after installing.
commands.shell_only_reason: Interactive setup — run in terminal with your API keys ready.

commands.title: Pipe text through a Fabric AI pattern
commands.description: Pipes text through a Fabric pattern. 'extract_wisdom' pulls key insights from articles or videos. Other patterns: summarize, write_essay, explain_code, create_story. Pipe any text in.
commands.command: echo 'Your article or text here' | fabric --pattern extract_wisdom
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace the text or pipe a file: cat article.txt | fabric --pattern summarize

commands.title: List all Fabric patterns
commands.description: Lists all available Fabric AI patterns. There are 100+ patterns for summarising, writing, coding, security analysis, and much more.

commands.title: Install Shell-GPT (AI in your shell)
commands.description: Installs Shell-GPT (sgpt) — brings AI directly into your shell. Ask it to generate shell commands, explain commands, or have a chat, all without leaving the terminal.

commands.title: Generate a shell command with AI
commands.description: Asks Shell-GPT to generate a shell command for a task in plain English. Add --execute to run it immediately. Great for commands you can't quite remember.
commands.command: sgpt --shell "find all python files modified in the last 7 days"
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace the description with what you want to do.

commands.title: Explain a command with AI
commands.description: Pipes a command into Shell-GPT to get a plain-English explanation of what it does. Useful for understanding complex one-liners or unfamiliar commands.
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace the command string with the one you want explained.

commands.title: Use Shell-GPT with local Ollama
commands.description: Configures Shell-GPT to use a local Ollama model instead of OpenAI. Set these environment variables before running sgpt.
commands.command: export OPENAI_API_KEY=ollama && export OPENAI_API_BASE=http://localhost:11434/v1 && sgpt --model llama3 "Hello"
commands.shell_only_reason: Set the env vars in your .bashrc for persistence, then run sgpt normally.

commands.title: Install AnythingLLM (local RAG system)
commands.description: AnythingLLM is an all-in-one local AI app — RAG (chat with your documents), multiple users, multiple AI providers including Ollama. Download the Linux AppImage from the official site.
commands.shell_only_reason: Downloads and launches the app — run in your terminal.

commands.title: Install Groq Python client
commands.description: Installs the Groq Python library. Groq provides extremely fast cloud inference (often 500+ tokens/second) for open models like Llama 3, Mixtral. Free tier available.

commands.title: Test Groq API (fastest LLM inference)
commands.description: Sends a test message to the Groq API. Groq uses custom LPU hardware for extremely fast inference — often 10x faster than GPU. Get your free API key at console.groq.com.
commands.command:
python3 -c "
from groq import Groq
client = Groq()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model='llama-3.1-8b-instant',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Hello!'}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
"
commands.shell_only_reason: Requires GROQ_API_KEY environment variable. Get it free at console.groq.com

commands.title: Install GitHub Copilot in CLI
commands.description: Installs the GitHub Copilot extension for the GitHub CLI. Lets you ask Copilot to explain commands, suggest shell commands, and answer questions right in the terminal.

commands.title: Ask GitHub Copilot to suggest a command
commands.description: Asks GitHub Copilot in the CLI to suggest a shell command for a task in plain English. It will explain what the command does and ask before running it.
commands.command: gh copilot suggest "undo the last git commit without losing my changes"
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace the description with your task. Requires GitHub Copilot subscription.

commands.title: Ask GitHub Copilot to explain a command
commands.description: Asks Copilot in the CLI to explain what a command does in plain English.
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace the command with the one you want explained.

commands.title: Set OpenAI API key (permanent)
commands.description: Adds your OpenAI API key to your shell profile so it's available in every session. Replace sk-... with your actual key from platform.openai.com.
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace sk-your-key-here with your actual OpenAI API key.

commands.title: Set Anthropic API key (permanent)
commands.description: Adds your Anthropic API key to your shell profile so Claude is available in every session. Get your key at console.anthropic.com.
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace with your actual Anthropic API key from console.anthropic.com

commands.title: Set Gemini API key (permanent)
commands.description: Adds your Google Gemini API key to your shell profile. Get a free key at aistudio.google.com. Very generous free tier with fast Gemini Flash model.
commands.shell_only_reason: Replace with your actual Gemini API key from aistudio.google.com

commands.title: Install ChromaDB (local vector database)
commands.description: Installs ChromaDB — the most popular local vector database for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems. Store and query embeddings to let AI chat with your documents.

commands.title: Install FAISS (fast vector search)
commands.description: Installs Facebook's FAISS — extremely fast similarity search for vector embeddings. Used in large-scale RAG systems and semantic search. CPU version.

commands.title: Install LlamaIndex (RAG framework)
commands.description: Installs LlamaIndex — a framework for building RAG applications. Connect AI to your PDFs, databases, APIs, and any data source. Works with Ollama and all major providers.

commands.title: Sync folder to another location
commands.description: Copies a folder to a destination, only transferring files that changed. The trailing slash on source means 'copy contents, not the folder itself'. Great for backups to an external drive.

commands.title: Mirror folder (delete removed files)
commands.description: Syncs a folder and also deletes files from the destination that no longer exist in the source. Creates a true mirror. Use with care — deleted files are gone.

commands.title: Sync to remote server over SSH
commands.description: Syncs a local folder to a remote server using SSH for transport. Replace user@server with your SSH target. Works the same as local rsync but tunnelled.

commands.title: Sync folder, excluding patterns
commands.description: Syncs a folder while skipping certain file types or directories. Add more --exclude options as needed. Useful for excluding caches, node_modules, .git, etc.

commands.title: Initialize a restic backup repository
commands.description: Creates a new restic backup repository at the given path. You'll set an encryption password. The repository can be on a local disk, USB drive, SFTP server, or S3/B2 bucket.

commands.title: Create a restic snapshot
commands.description: Backs up one or more directories into a restic repository. Creates a deduplicated, encrypted snapshot. Fast for incremental backups — only changed data is transferred.

commands.title: List all restic snapshots
commands.description: Shows all backup snapshots stored in a restic repository, including when each was taken and what paths were backed up.

commands.title: Restore from a restic snapshot
commands.description: Restores files from a specific restic snapshot to a target directory. Replace 'latest' with a snapshot ID from 'restic snapshots' to restore a specific point in time.

commands.title: Prune old restic snapshots
commands.description: Removes old snapshots and the data only referenced by them, keeping the last 7 daily, 4 weekly, and 12 monthly snapshots. Frees up space in the repository.

commands.title: Initialize a BorgBackup repository
commands.description: Creates a new Borg repository with repokey encryption. BorgBackup is excellent for automated server backups — deduplicated, compressed, and encrypted.

commands.title: Create a BorgBackup archive
commands.description: Creates a compressed and deduplicated Borg archive. The ::hostname-date part is the archive name. --stats shows space usage. --progress shows files as they are processed.

commands.title: List BorgBackup archives
commands.description: Lists all archives stored in a Borg repository with their creation time and size.

commands.title: Install rclone (cloud sync tool)
commands.description: Installs rclone — the Swiss Army knife for cloud storage. Works with Google Drive, Dropbox, S3, Backblaze B2, OneDrive, SFTP, and 40+ more providers.

commands.title: Configure rclone cloud provider
commands.description: Launches rclone's interactive setup wizard to add a new cloud storage provider. Walk through the prompts to connect Google Drive, Dropbox, S3, etc.

commands.title: Sync local folder to cloud with rclone
commands.description: Syncs a local folder to a cloud storage remote. Replace 'gdrive' with your configured remote name. Files deleted locally are also deleted in the cloud.

commands.title: Copy local folder to cloud with rclone
commands.description: Copies a local folder to cloud storage without deleting anything in the destination. Safe option when you want to add files without risking deletion.

commands.title: Mount cloud storage as local folder
commands.description: Mounts a cloud storage remote as a local directory. You can then browse and open files as if they were local. Requires FUSE. Unmount with fusermount -u ~/cloud.

commands.title: Create a compressed tar archive
commands.description: Creates a .tar.gz (gzip) compressed archive of a folder. -c=create, -z=gzip, -v=verbose (show files), -f=filename. Use -j for bzip2 or -J for xz compression instead.

commands.title: Extract a tar archive
commands.description: Extracts a .tar.gz archive. -x=extract, -z=gzip (auto-detected), -v=verbose, -f=file. Works with .tar.gz, .tar.bz2, .tar.xz. Add -C /target/ to extract to a different directory.

commands.title: Install KVM and libvirt
commands.description: Installs KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine), libvirt, QEMU, and virt-manager GUI. This is the best way to run VMs on Linux — hardware-level virtualisation with near-native performance.
commands.command: sudo apt install qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-system libvirt-clients bridge-utils virt-manager

commands.title: Check if hardware supports KVM
commands.description: Checks if your CPU supports hardware virtualisation (required for KVM). Should output a number greater than 0. If 0, check BIOS to enable Intel VT-x or AMD-V.

commands.title: Add user to libvirt group
commands.description: Adds your user to the libvirt and kvm groups so you can manage VMs without sudo. Log out and back in for the change to take effect.

commands.title: List all VMs
commands.description: Lists all virtual machines managed by libvirt, showing their state (running, shut off, paused). --all shows VMs that are not running.

commands.title: Start a VM
commands.description: Starts a virtual machine by name. Find the name with 'virsh list --all'. The VM starts in the background — connect with virt-manager or virsh console.

commands.title: Gracefully shut down a VM
commands.description: Sends a shutdown signal to a VM (like pressing the power button). The guest OS handles the shutdown cleanly. Use 'virsh destroy' to force-stop if unresponsive.

commands.title: Force-stop a VM (hard power off)
commands.description: Immediately cuts power to a VM without a graceful shutdown. Use only if the VM is stuck and won't respond to virsh shutdown. Data loss may occur.

commands.title: Take a VM snapshot
commands.description: Creates a snapshot of a VM's current state. You can revert to this snapshot later with 'virsh snapshot-revert'. Great before risky changes.

commands.title: Revert VM to a snapshot
commands.description: Restores a VM to a previously saved snapshot state. All changes made after the snapshot was taken are discarded.

commands.title: Create a new VM from ISO
commands.description: Creates and starts a new VM using virt-install. Installs from an ISO file. Adjust RAM (--ram), CPUs, disk size (--disk size=), and ISO path as needed.

commands.title: Clone an existing VM
commands.description: Creates a complete copy of an existing VM under a new name. Useful for quickly provisioning similar systems from a base template.

commands.title: Connect to VM console via terminal
commands.description: Connects to a VM's serial console directly in the terminal (no GUI needed). Works for headless VMs. Press Ctrl+] to exit the console.

commands.title: Install VirtualBox
commands.description: Installs Oracle VirtualBox — another popular VM platform, more user-friendly than KVM but with slightly lower performance. Good for desktop use.

commands.title: List VirtualBox VMs
commands.description: Lists all VirtualBox virtual machines. 'VBoxManage list runningvms' shows only the currently running ones.

commands.title: Start VirtualBox VM headless
commands.description: Starts a VirtualBox VM in headless mode (no GUI window). Useful for running VMs in the background. Connect to it with RDP or SSH.

commands.title: Quick boot ISO with QEMU (no install)
commands.description: Boots directly from an ISO file with QEMU without creating a persistent VM. Great for testing a live Linux distro or rescue disk. Press Ctrl+Alt+G to release mouse.

commands.title: Install WireGuard
commands.description: Installs WireGuard — the modern, fast, and simple VPN protocol. Much simpler to configure than OpenVPN and faster in benchmarks. Built into the Linux kernel since 5.6.

commands.title: Generate WireGuard key pair
commands.description: Generates a private and public key pair for WireGuard. The private key stays on this machine; the public key is shared with peers. Store the private key securely.
commands.command: wg genkey | tee privatekey | wg pubkey > publickey && echo 'Private:' && cat privatekey && echo 'Public:' && cat publickey

commands.title: Bring up WireGuard interface
commands.description: Activates a WireGuard VPN connection using a config file. The config is typically at /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf and contains your private key and peer info.

commands.title: Bring down WireGuard interface
commands.description: Disconnects the WireGuard VPN and removes the network interface. Use 'wg show' to check the connection status before and after.

commands.title: Show WireGuard status
commands.description: Displays the current WireGuard interface status, including connected peers, their last handshake time, and data transferred. Great for diagnosing connection issues.

commands.title: Enable WireGuard on system boot
commands.description: Enables the WireGuard interface to automatically come up when the system boots. Uses systemd. The interface name (wg0) must match your config file name.

commands.title: Install OpenVPN client
commands.description: Installs the OpenVPN client. Many corporate VPNs and VPS providers use OpenVPN. You'll need a .ovpn config file from your VPN provider to connect.

commands.title: Connect to OpenVPN with config file
commands.description: Connects to an OpenVPN server using a .ovpn configuration file from your VPN provider. Run as root or with sudo. Press Ctrl+C to disconnect.

commands.title: Create SSH SOCKS5 proxy (dynamic tunnel)
commands.description: Creates a local SOCKS5 proxy on port 1080 through an SSH server. Configure your browser to use SOCKS5 localhost:1080 and all traffic routes through the remote server.

commands.title: SSH local port forwarding
commands.description: Forwards a local port to a port on a remote machine through SSH. E.g. access a remote database at localhost:5432 even if it's not publicly exposed. -N means no shell.

commands.title: SSH remote port forwarding
commands.description: Exposes a local port on a remote server. Useful for temporarily exposing a local development server to the internet through a remote machine.

commands.title: Check your current public IP address
commands.description: Displays your current public IP address. Run this before and after connecting to a VPN to verify the VPN is routing your traffic correctly.

commands.title: Encrypt a partition with LUKS
commands.description: Formats a block device with LUKS encryption. WARNING: This destroys all data on the device. Use lsblk to identify the correct device first. Never run on the wrong disk.

commands.title: Open (unlock) a LUKS volume
commands.description: Unlocks a LUKS-encrypted partition and maps it to a name you choose (e.g. 'mydata'). The unlocked device appears at /dev/mapper/mydata and can then be mounted.

commands.title: Close a LUKS volume
commands.description: Locks and unmounts a LUKS volume. Always close before physically removing an encrypted drive.

commands.title: Check LUKS volume status
commands.description: Shows the status of an opened LUKS volume — cipher, key size, offset, and whether it's active.

commands.title: Add a new LUKS passphrase
commands.description: Adds an additional passphrase to a LUKS volume. LUKS supports up to 8 key slots — useful for setting up a recovery key or allowing multiple users.

commands.title: Install age (modern file encryption)
commands.description: Installs age — a simple, modern, and secure file encryption tool. Much simpler than GPG. Encrypt with a public key or a passphrase.

commands.title: Encrypt a file with age
commands.description: Encrypts a file using age. -r specifies the recipient's public key (age1...) or use -p for a passphrase prompt. The result is an .age file.

commands.title: Decrypt an age-encrypted file
commands.description: Decrypts an age-encrypted file using your private key (identity file). The -i flag specifies the identity file. Use -d flag with output redirection.

commands.title: Encrypt a file with GPG
commands.description: Encrypts a file using GPG with AES-256 symmetric encryption and a passphrase. The output file will have a .gpg extension. No key setup required.

commands.title: Decrypt a GPG file
commands.description: Decrypts a GPG-encrypted file. GPG will prompt for the passphrase. The decrypted output goes to the original filename (without .gpg).

commands.title: Securely delete a file
commands.description: Overwrites a file multiple times before deleting to prevent recovery. More secure than 'rm' but not guaranteed on SSDs/flash drives due to wear levelling. For SSDs use disk encryption instead.

commands.title: List all block devices and partitions
commands.description: Shows all block devices (disks, partitions, loop devices) in a tree layout with sizes and mount points. One of the most useful commands before doing any disk work.

commands.title: Open disk with parted (partition editor)
commands.description: Launches GNU parted for the specified disk. Type 'print' to see current partition table, 'help' for all commands. Replace /dev/sdb with your target disk.

commands.title: Format partition as ext4
commands.description: Formats a partition with the ext4 filesystem — the standard Linux filesystem. Replace /dev/sdX1 with your partition. WARNING: this destroys all data on the partition.

commands.title: Format partition as btrfs
commands.description: Formats a partition with btrfs — a modern copy-on-write filesystem with built-in snapshots, RAID, and compression. Increasingly popular on modern Linux systems.

commands.title: Create a btrfs subvolume snapshot
commands.description: Creates a read-write snapshot of a btrfs subvolume. Snapshots are near-instant and take no extra space until data diverges. Great for pre-update checkpoints.

commands.title: List btrfs subvolumes
commands.description: Lists all subvolumes and snapshots on a btrfs filesystem mount point.

commands.title: Enable btrfs compression on a directory
commands.description: Enables transparent zstd compression on a directory and re-compresses existing files. zstd offers an excellent balance of speed and compression ratio.
commands.command: sudo btrfs property set /data compression zstd

commands.title: List LVM physical volumes
commands.description: Displays all physical volumes in the LVM setup — the raw block devices or partitions that have been added to LVM.

commands.title: List LVM volume groups
commands.description: Displays all LVM volume groups, their size, and free space. Volume groups pool together physical volumes into one large storage pool.

commands.title: List LVM logical volumes
commands.description: Displays all LVM logical volumes — the virtual partitions carved out of volume groups. These are what you format and mount.

commands.title: Extend an LVM logical volume
commands.description: Grows a logical volume by a specified amount and also resizes the filesystem inside it. Replace vg0/lv0 with your volume group and logical volume names.

commands.title: Mount an NTFS partition (Windows drive)
commands.description: Installs ntfs-3g driver and mounts an NTFS partition (Windows drive) with full read-write access. Replace /dev/sdX1 and /mnt/windows as needed.
commands.command: sudo apt install ntfs-3g && sudo mount -t ntfs-3g /dev/sdX1 /mnt/windows

commands.title: Check and repair filesystem (fsck)
commands.description: Checks and optionally repairs a filesystem for errors. Run only on unmounted filesystems. -y automatically answers yes to repairs. Use lsblk to find the device.

commands.title: Update GRUB bootloader config
commands.description: Regenerates the GRUB configuration file — run this after installing a new kernel, changing /etc/default/grub settings, or adding a new OS. Required for changes to take effect.

commands.title: Reinstall GRUB to a disk
commands.description: Re-installs the GRUB bootloader to the MBR/EFI partition of a disk. Run this when GRUB is broken (e.g. after reinstalling Windows). Replace /dev/sda with your boot disk.

commands.title: Change GRUB boot menu timeout
commands.description: Edits the GRUB timeout (seconds to show the menu before auto-booting). Set GRUB_TIMEOUT=0 to skip the menu entirely, or -1 to wait forever. Then run update-grub.

commands.title: List installed kernels
commands.description: Lists all installed Linux kernels on the system. Useful when you want to remove old kernels to free up space in /boot.

commands.title: List EFI boot entries
commands.description: Lists all EFI boot entries registered in the UEFI firmware. Shows which OS/bootloaders the firmware knows about and their order.

commands.title: Install systemd-boot (alternative to GRUB)
commands.description: Installs systemd-boot (formerly gummiboot) as the EFI bootloader. Simpler than GRUB, fast, and integrated with systemd. Only works on UEFI systems.

commands.title: Enter emergency/rescue mode
commands.description: Reboots into systemd emergency mode (minimal, root shell) to diagnose serious boot problems. Useful when the system won't boot normally.

commands.title: Start a new named tmux session
commands.description: Creates a new tmux session with a name. Naming sessions makes it easy to reattach later. Inside tmux: Ctrl+B is the prefix for all commands.

commands.title: Attach to an existing tmux session
commands.description: Reattaches to a running tmux session by name. If you only have one session, 'tmux attach' works without the -t flag.

commands.title: List all tmux sessions
commands.description: Shows all running tmux sessions with their IDs, names, and creation times. Use this to find the name to attach to.

commands.title: Kill a tmux session
commands.description: Terminates a tmux session and all processes running inside it. Use 'tmux kill-server' to stop all sessions at once.

commands.title: Split tmux pane horizontally
commands.description: Splits the current pane into two side-by-side panes. Prefix is Ctrl+B. In tmux you can also press Ctrl+B then % to split horizontally.

commands.title: Split tmux pane vertically
commands.description: Splits the current pane into two stacked panes (one above the other). In tmux you can also press Ctrl+B then " to split vertically.

commands.title: Create a new tmux window (tab)
commands.description: Creates a new window (like a new tab) in the current tmux session. Switch between windows with Ctrl+B then the window number, or Ctrl+B n/p for next/previous.

commands.title: Rename current tmux window
commands.description: Renames the current window in the tmux status bar. Useful when you have many windows open and want to track what each one is for.

commands.title: Send a command to a tmux pane
commands.description: Runs a command in a specific tmux pane from outside tmux. Useful in scripts to automate running commands in tmux sessions.

commands.title: Enter tmux copy mode (scroll back)
commands.description: Enters copy mode where you can scroll up through the terminal history using arrow keys or Vim keys. Press q to exit. Use Ctrl+B [ shortcut in a live session.

commands.title: Edit tmux configuration
commands.description: Opens the tmux config file. Common settings: change the prefix key, set vi keys in copy mode, enable mouse support (set -g mouse on), customise the status bar.

commands.title: Reload tmux configuration
commands.description: Reloads the tmux config file without restarting. Run this inside tmux after editing ~/.tmux.conf for changes to take effect immediately.

commands.title: Bash script shebang line
commands.description: The first line of every bash script. Tells the OS to use bash to run this file. After adding the shebang, make it executable with: chmod +x script.sh

commands.title: Enable strict mode in bash scripts
commands.description: These three options make bash scripts safer: -e exits on error, -u treats unset variables as errors, -o pipefail fails if any command in a pipe fails. Put this at the top of every script.

commands.title: Bash variable assignment and use
commands.description: How to define and use variables in bash. No spaces around =. Use $VAR or ${VAR} to reference. ${VAR:-default} gives a default if VAR is unset.

commands.title: Bash if/else conditional
commands.description: Basic if/else structure in bash. Common tests: -f file (file exists), -d dir (directory exists), -z string (empty), -n string (not empty), [ a = b ] (string equals).
commands.command:
if [ -f "/etc/hosts" ]; then
  echo "hosts file exists"
else
  echo "no hosts file"
fi

commands.title: Bash for loop (iterate list)
commands.description: Loops over a list of items. The list can be files (*.txt), a range ({1..10}), command output ($(ls)), or an explicit list.
commands.command:
for item in one two three; do
  echo "Item: $item"
done

commands.title: Bash while loop
commands.description: Repeats a block while a condition is true. 'while read line' is very common for processing lines of a file or command output one by one.
commands.command:
while read line; do
  echo "Got: $line"
done < /etc/hosts

commands.title: Define a bash function
commands.description: Defines a reusable function in bash. $1, $2, etc. are positional arguments. $@ means all arguments. Functions are called just like commands.

commands.title: Bash array operations
commands.description: How to create, access, and iterate arrays in bash. Arrays are zero-indexed. ${arr[@]} expands all elements. ${#arr[@]} gives the count.
commands.command:
arr=(one two three)
echo ${arr[0]}    # first element
echo ${arr[@]}   # all elements
echo ${#arr[@]}  # count

commands.title: Bash process substitution
commands.description: Process substitution <(cmd) lets you pass the output of a command as if it were a file. Useful when a command needs file arguments but you want to use command output.

commands.title: Bash heredoc (multi-line string)
commands.description: Heredoc lets you write multi-line strings in bash. Everything between <<'EOF' and EOF is treated as a string. Single-quoted EOF prevents variable expansion; double-quoted allows it.
commands.command:
cat <<'EOF'
This is a
multi-line
string
EOF

commands.title: Bash trap (cleanup on exit/error)
commands.description: trap runs a command when the script exits, regardless of how it exits (normal exit, error, Ctrl+C). Useful for cleaning up temp files or printing error messages.
commands.command: trap 'echo "Script failed at line $LINENO"; rm -f /tmp/mytemp' ERR EXIT

commands.title: Debug a bash script
commands.description: Runs a bash script in debug mode — prints each command before executing it. Extremely useful for finding where a script fails. You can also add 'set -x' inside the script.

commands.title: Bash regex matching with =~
commands.description: Tests if a string matches a regex using bash's built-in =~ operator. No quotes around the regex. Captured groups are in BASH_REMATCH array.

commands.title: Install Nginx web server
commands.description: Installs Nginx — a high-performance web server and reverse proxy. Used for serving websites, load balancing, and proxying requests to backend apps (Node.js, Python, etc.).
commands.command: sudo apt install nginx && sudo systemctl enable nginx && sudo systemctl start nginx

commands.title: Test Nginx configuration
commands.description: Validates the Nginx configuration files for syntax errors before reloading. Always run this before reloading Nginx to avoid breaking a running server.

commands.title: Reload Nginx (apply config changes)
commands.description: Reloads Nginx's configuration without dropping active connections. Use this after editing a site config. 'restart' would briefly interrupt traffic.

commands.title: Enable an Nginx site
commands.description: Creates a symlink from sites-available to sites-enabled to activate a virtual host config. Replace mysite with your config filename (without .conf).
commands.command: sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/mysite /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ && sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

commands.title: Install Apache web server
commands.description: Installs the Apache 2 web server. Apache is the most widely deployed web server, great for shared hosting and .htaccess based configuration.
commands.command: sudo apt install apache2 && sudo systemctl enable apache2 && sudo systemctl start apache2

commands.title: Enable Apache module
commands.description: Enables a module in Apache2 and reloads the server. Common modules: rewrite (URL rewriting), ssl (HTTPS), headers, proxy. Disabling: a2dismod.
commands.command: sudo a2enmod rewrite && sudo systemctl reload apache2

commands.title: Install Certbot (free HTTPS certificates)
commands.description: Installs Certbot to get free Let's Encrypt SSL/TLS certificates for your domain. Makes your site HTTPS. Automatically handles renewal.

commands.title: Get a free SSL certificate for a domain
commands.description: Requests a Let's Encrypt certificate for your domain and automatically configures Nginx to use it. Replace example.com with your domain. Your server must be publicly reachable.

commands.title: Renew Let's Encrypt certificates
commands.description: Renews all Let's Encrypt certificates that are near expiry. Certbot sets up a cron job to do this automatically, but you can run it manually to test.

commands.title: Serve current directory over HTTP (Python)
commands.description: Starts a simple HTTP file server on port 8000 in the current directory. Useful for quickly sharing files on a local network or testing HTML files. No installation needed.

commands.title: Install Caddy web server
commands.description: Installs Caddy — a modern web server that automatically gets and renews HTTPS certificates. Its config (Caddyfile) is much simpler than Nginx or Apache.
commands.command: sudo apt install -y debian-keyring debian-archive-keyring apt-transport-https && curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/gpg.key' | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/caddy-stable-archive-keyring.gpg && curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/debian.deb.txt' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/caddy-stable.list && sudo apt update && sudo apt install caddy

commands.title: Install xRDP (Windows RDP server for Linux)
commands.description: Installs xRDP, which allows Windows Remote Desktop (RDP) clients to connect to your Linux desktop. Great for accessing Linux from Windows using the built-in Remote Desktop app.
commands.command: sudo apt install xrdp && sudo systemctl enable xrdp && sudo systemctl start xrdp

commands.title: Fix xRDP black screen on Ubuntu
commands.description: Fixes the common black screen issue when connecting via RDP to Ubuntu. Edits the xRDP session start script to use the correct desktop session.
commands.command:
echo 'export GNOME_SHELL_SESSION_MODE=ubuntu
export XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=ubuntu:GNOME
export XDG_SESSION_TYPE=x11' > ~/.xsessionrc

commands.title: Install TigerVNC server
commands.description: Installs TigerVNC — a fast VNC server for Linux. VNC lets you see and control the Linux desktop from any VNC client (Windows, Mac, phone).

commands.title: Start VNC server session
commands.description: Starts a VNC server on display :1 (port 5901). Sets resolution to 1920x1080. First run will ask you to set a VNC password. Connect with any VNC viewer to your-ip:5901.

commands.title: Stop VNC server session
commands.description: Stops a running VNC server on a specific display number.

commands.title: Tunnel VNC over SSH (secure)
commands.description: Creates an SSH tunnel to forward VNC traffic securely. VNC is unencrypted by default — always tunnel through SSH when connecting over the internet. Then connect your VNC client to localhost:5901.

commands.title: Share current desktop session with x11vnc
commands.description: Shares your current (already running) desktop session via VNC. Unlike TigerVNC which creates a new session, x11vnc mirrors what's currently on screen. Password required on first run with -storepasswd.

commands.title: Install nvm (Node Version Manager)
commands.description: Installs nvm — lets you install and switch between multiple Node.js versions without sudo. The most popular way to manage Node on Linux. Restart your shell after installing.

commands.title: Install a Node.js version with nvm
commands.description: Installs a specific Node.js version and sets it as the current version. Use 'nvm ls-remote' to see all available versions. 'lts' installs the latest LTS version.

commands.title: List installed Node.js versions
commands.description: Shows all Node.js versions installed via nvm, with the current active version highlighted. 'nvm ls-remote' shows all downloadable versions.

commands.title: Switch Node.js version with nvm
commands.description: Switches the active Node.js version for the current shell session. To set a default version, use 'nvm alias default 20'.

commands.title: Install pyenv (Python Version Manager)
commands.description: Installs pyenv — lets you install and switch between multiple Python versions. Much better than using the system Python or managing conda environments.

commands.title: Install a Python version with pyenv
commands.description: Downloads and compiles a specific Python version. Use 'pyenv install --list' to see all available versions. This may take a few minutes to compile.

commands.title: List Python versions (pyenv)
commands.description: Lists all Python versions installed via pyenv, showing which is currently active globally and locally.

commands.title: Install SDKMAN (Java/Groovy/Kotlin manager)
commands.description: Installs SDKMAN — the best way to manage Java, Groovy, Kotlin, Gradle, Maven, and other JVM tools on Linux. Handles multiple versions cleanly.

commands.title: Install a Java version with SDKMAN
commands.description: Installs a specific Java version via SDKMAN. 'sdk list java' shows all available distributions (OpenJDK, GraalVM, Corretto, Temurin). The identifier format is version+distro.

commands.title: Install mise (universal version manager)
commands.description: Installs mise (formerly rtx) — a fast, universal version manager for Node, Python, Ruby, Go, Java, and 100+ more tools. Written in Rust, much faster than asdf.

commands.title: Install ffmpeg
commands.description: Installs ffmpeg — the most powerful open-source tool for audio/video conversion, transcoding, streaming, and processing. Used by almost every media app under the hood.

commands.title: Convert video to MP4 (H.264)
commands.description: Converts any video file to MP4 with H.264 video and AAC audio — the most universally compatible format. ffmpeg auto-detects the input format. Output quality is controlled with -crf (18=high quality, 28=smaller file).

commands.title: Extract audio from video (ffmpeg)
commands.description: Extracts the audio track from a video file into a separate audio file without re-encoding (-c:a copy means copy the audio stream as-is).

commands.title: Compress video to smaller file size
commands.description: Reduces video file size by re-encoding with a higher CRF value (28 vs the default 23). Bigger CRF = smaller file, lower quality. Good for sharing or storing on limited space.

commands.title: Take screenshot from video at timestamp
commands.description: Captures a single frame from a video at a specific timestamp as a PNG image. -ss is the seek time (HH:MM:SS), -frames:v 1 grabs one frame.

commands.title: Convert video clip to GIF
commands.description: Converts a short video clip to an animated GIF. -t 5 takes 5 seconds from the -ss start point. Generates a palette first for better quality GIFs.

commands.title: Resize video resolution (ffmpeg)
commands.description: Scales a video to a new resolution. -1 on the height means 'maintain aspect ratio'. Common targets: 1280:720 (720p), 1920:1080 (1080p), 640:-1 (640px wide).

commands.title: Install yt-dlp (video downloader)
commands.description: Installs yt-dlp — the most capable open-source video downloader. Works with YouTube, Vimeo, Twitter/X, Instagram, TikTok, and 1000+ sites. A maintained fork of youtube-dl.

commands.title: Download a video with yt-dlp
commands.description: Downloads a video in the best available quality. yt-dlp works with YouTube, Vimeo, and 1000+ other sites. The URL is pasted after the command.

commands.title: Download audio only (MP3) with yt-dlp
commands.description: Downloads only the audio from a video and converts it to MP3. Great for saving music or podcasts. Requires ffmpeg to be installed for the conversion.

commands.title: Download a YouTube playlist
commands.description: Downloads all videos in a YouTube playlist. Use --playlist-start and --playlist-end to download a range. '--yes-playlist' confirms playlist download.

commands.title: Install ImageMagick
commands.description: Installs ImageMagick — the classic command-line image processing suite. Convert formats, resize, crop, add text, apply filters, create thumbnails, and more.

commands.title: Convert image format (ImageMagick)
commands.description: Converts an image from one format to another. ImageMagick supports JPG, PNG, WEBP, BMP, GIF, TIFF, and many more. Just change the extension.

commands.title: Resize an image (ImageMagick)
commands.description: Resizes an image to a specific width, maintaining aspect ratio (the ! forces exact dimensions ignoring ratio). Use 50% for percentage scaling.

commands.title: Bulk resize all images in a folder
commands.description: Resizes all JPG images in a folder and saves them to an 'output' subfolder. The mogrify command works in-place — use convert in a loop for safer batch processing.
commands.command: mkdir -p output && for f in *.jpg; do convert "$f" -resize 1920x1080\> "output/$f"; done

commands.title: Install PDF command-line tools
commands.description: Installs a collection of PDF tools: pdftk (merge/split/rotate), poppler-utils (pdfinfo/pdftotext/pdfimages), ghostscript (compress/convert), and pandoc (document conversion).
commands.command: sudo apt install pdftk poppler-utils ghostscript pandoc

commands.title: Merge multiple PDFs into one
commands.description: Combines multiple PDF files into a single PDF in the order specified. pdftk is the most reliable tool for this. Replace input1.pdf input2.pdf with your files.
commands.command: pdftk input1.pdf input2.pdf input3.pdf cat output merged.pdf

commands.title: Split PDF into individual pages
commands.description: Splits each page of a PDF into a separate file. Output files are named page_01.pdf, page_02.pdf, etc.

commands.title: Compress a PDF with Ghostscript
commands.description: Reduces PDF file size using Ghostscript. '/ebook' balances quality and size; options from smallest to biggest: /screen /ebook /printer /prepress. Great for emailing large PDFs.

commands.title: Extract text from a PDF
commands.description: Extracts all text content from a PDF file into a plain text file. Useful for searching PDF content, feeding PDFs to AI, or extracting data.

commands.title: Show PDF metadata and info
commands.description: Displays metadata about a PDF: number of pages, creator, creation date, page size, encryption status, etc.

commands.title: Rotate PDF pages
commands.description: Rotates all pages of a PDF by 90 degrees clockwise. Use '1-endwest' to rotate all pages. Directions: north (180), east (90cw), west (90ccw), south (180).

commands.title: Add OCR text layer to scanned PDF
commands.description: Installs ocrmypdf and adds an OCR layer to a scanned PDF, making it searchable and copy-pasteable. Supports 100+ languages. One of the most useful PDF tools available.
commands.command: sudo apt install ocrmypdf && ocrmypdf input-scanned.pdf output-searchable.pdf

commands.title: Convert documents with Pandoc
commands.description: Pandoc converts between almost any document format: Markdown, HTML, DOCX, PDF, EPUB, LaTeX, RST, and more. This example converts Markdown to PDF (requires LaTeX) or DOCX.

commands.title: Convert Markdown to HTML (Pandoc)
commands.description: Converts a Markdown file to a standalone HTML file with embedded CSS. --standalone adds proper HTML headers. Great for turning README files into web pages.

commands.title: Install Samba (share files with Windows)
commands.description: Installs Samba — allows Linux to share folders with Windows computers on the same network using the SMB protocol. Windows will see your shares in File Explorer.

commands.title: Add a Samba share to config
commands.description: Opens the Samba configuration file to add a new share. Add a block at the bottom: [ShareName] path = /path/to/folder browseable = yes writable = yes guest ok = no

commands.title: Add a Samba user
commands.description: Creates a Samba password for a user. The user must already exist as a Linux user. This Samba password can be different from the Linux login password.

commands.title: Restart Samba services
commands.description: Restarts the Samba services after making configuration changes. Both smbd (file sharing) and nmbd (name resolution) need to restart.

commands.title: Install NFS server
commands.description: Installs the NFS server for sharing folders between Linux machines. NFS is faster than Samba for Linux-to-Linux file sharing.

commands.title: Add an NFS export (share a folder)
commands.description: Adds a folder to the NFS exports file. 192.168.1.0/24 allows access from your local network. Options: rw (read-write), ro (read-only), sync (safe), async (faster but risky).

commands.title: Mount an NFS share
commands.description: Mounts a remote NFS share onto a local directory. Replace server-ip with the server's IP and /remote/path with the exported path.

commands.title: Install SSHFS (mount remote folders)
commands.description: Installs SSHFS — lets you mount a remote folder over SSH as if it were a local directory. No server setup needed if you have SSH access. Great for editing remote files locally.

commands.title: Mount remote folder with SSHFS
commands.description: Mounts a remote directory over SSH onto a local mount point. Once mounted, you can browse and edit files as if they were local. Use fusermount -u ~/remotedir to unmount.

commands.title: List all iptables rules
commands.description: Shows all current iptables firewall rules with line numbers. -n prevents slow DNS lookups. -v shows packet/byte counters. Essential for understanding current firewall state.

commands.title: Allow incoming traffic on a port
commands.description: Adds an iptables rule to accept incoming TCP traffic on a specific port. Replace 8080 with your port and tcp with udp if needed. Run iptables-save to persist across reboots.

commands.title: Block all traffic from an IP address
commands.description: Drops all incoming traffic from a specific IP address. Useful for blocking an attacker or a known bad actor. Add multiple rules for multiple IPs.

commands.title: Save iptables rules (persist reboots)
commands.description: Saves current iptables rules so they survive a reboot. Requires the iptables-persistent package. Alternatively use: sudo iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4
commands.command: sudo apt install iptables-persistent && sudo netfilter-persistent save

commands.title: Enable UFW firewall
commands.description: Enables UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) — a user-friendly frontend to iptables. UFW is the recommended firewall tool on Ubuntu. Always allow SSH first to avoid locking yourself out.
commands.command: sudo ufw allow ssh && sudo ufw enable && sudo ufw status verbose

commands.title: Allow a port through UFW
commands.description: Opens a port in the UFW firewall. You can specify a port number, a service name (/etc/services), or a named profile. 'sudo ufw deny 23' to block instead.

commands.title: Create a network bridge
commands.description: Creates a network bridge — a virtual switch that connects multiple network interfaces. Used by KVM/VMs and Docker for networking. Replace eth0 with your actual interface name.
commands.command: sudo ip link add name br0 type bridge && sudo ip link set eth0 master br0 && sudo ip link set br0 up

commands.title: Create a VLAN interface
commands.description: Creates a VLAN-tagged interface on top of a physical interface. VLAN 10 on eth0 appears as eth0.10. Requires the 8021q kernel module.
commands.command: sudo modprobe 8021q && sudo ip link add link eth0 name eth0.10 type vlan id 10 && sudo ip link set eth0.10 up

commands.title: Test network bandwidth with iperf3
commands.description: Tests network bandwidth between two machines. On the server: 'iperf3 -s'. On the client: run this command with the server's IP. Shows throughput in Mbps/Gbps.

commands.title: Show all listening ports (ss)
commands.description: Lists all ports the system is currently listening on, with the process name. ss is the modern replacement for netstat. -t=TCP -u=UDP -l=listening -p=process -n=numeric.

commands.title: Capture network packets with tcpdump
commands.description: Captures network packets on an interface and saves to a .pcap file for analysis in Wireshark. -i any captures all interfaces. -c 100 stops after 100 packets. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

commands.title: Print specific columns with awk
commands.description: awk splits each line into fields (by whitespace or a delimiter). $1 is first field, $2 second, etc. -F sets the delimiter. This prints the username and shell from /etc/passwd.

commands.title: Filter lines matching a pattern (awk)
commands.description: awk can both filter and transform. /pattern/ matches lines containing that pattern. This prints only lines where the 3rd field is greater than 1000.

commands.title: Sum a column of numbers (awk)
commands.description: Adds up all values in the first column of a file. BEGIN runs before processing, END runs after. This pattern works for any simple column sum.

commands.title: Replace text in a file (sed)
commands.description: Replaces all occurrences of a pattern in a file. -i edits the file in-place. /g means replace all occurrences per line (not just the first). Without -i, output goes to stdout.

commands.title: Delete lines matching a pattern (sed)
commands.description: Deletes all lines containing a pattern from a file. d means delete. Combine with -n and p to instead print only matching lines (like grep).

commands.title: Extract a range of lines (sed)
commands.description: Prints lines 10 through 20 from a file without loading the whole file. -n suppresses default printing, p prints the matched range. Faster than head/tail for specific ranges.

commands.title: Run command on each input line (xargs)
commands.description: xargs takes lines from stdin and passes them as arguments to a command. -I{} lets you place the input anywhere in the command. Here: delete each file listed in files.txt.

commands.title: Run commands in parallel (xargs)
commands.description: Runs commands in parallel using xargs. -P 4 runs 4 processes at once. Great for speeding up operations on many files.

commands.title: Sort and deduplicate a file
commands.description: Sorts a file alphabetically and removes duplicate lines. sort | uniq is the classic combo. 'sort -u' is the shortcut. Add 'sort -rn' for reverse numerical sort.

commands.title: Count and rank occurrences
commands.description: Counts how many times each unique line appears and sorts by frequency. Classic log analysis pipeline: uniq -c counts, sort -rn sorts numerically in reverse (most common first).

commands.title: Extract fields from delimited text (cut)
commands.description: Extracts specific fields from delimited text. -d sets the delimiter, -f specifies field numbers. This extracts the first and third comma-separated fields.

commands.title: Translate or delete characters (tr)
commands.description: Replaces or deletes specific characters in a stream. This converts all lowercase to uppercase. Use tr -d '\n' to remove newlines, or tr -s ' ' to squeeze repeated spaces.

commands.title: Join files side by side (paste)
commands.description: Pastes two files side by side as columns, separated by a tab. Useful for combining data from separate files into a single table. -d',' changes the delimiter to a comma.

commands.title: Install lm-sensors (hardware temperatures)
commands.description: Installs lm-sensors for reading CPU, GPU, motherboard temperatures and fan speeds. Run 'sudo sensors-detect' once after installing to detect sensors.
commands.command: sudo apt install lm-sensors && sudo sensors-detect --auto

commands.title: Read hardware temperatures and fan speeds
commands.description: Displays current CPU/GPU temperatures, fan speeds, and voltage readings from all detected hardware sensors.

commands.title: Show NVIDIA GPU status
commands.description: Displays NVIDIA GPU temperature, VRAM usage, GPU utilisation percentage, and running processes. Requires nvidia-driver to be installed. Like htop but for your GPU.

commands.title: Show AMD GPU information
commands.description: Displays AMD GPU status — temperature, usage, VRAM, fan speed. radeontop provides real-time AMD GPU monitoring.

commands.title: Test hard drive speed (hdparm)
commands.description: Measures the read speed of a disk using hdparm. -t tests buffered reads. Replace /dev/sda with your drive. Good baseline: HDD ~100-200 MB/s, SSD 300-600, NVMe 1000-7000 MB/s.

commands.title: Show detailed CPU information
commands.description: Displays CPU model, core count, thread count, cache sizes, and supported instruction sets. 'lscpu' is the most readable way to see your CPU specs.

commands.title: Show RAM slots and module info
commands.description: Displays detailed information about installed RAM: slot locations, capacity, speed, and type (DDR4/DDR5). Useful for knowing what RAM you have and what slots are free.

commands.title: List all PCI devices
commands.description: Lists all PCI devices including GPU, network cards, sound cards, and controllers. Use lspci -v for verbose details, or lspci -k to see which kernel driver is loaded.

commands.title: List all USB devices
commands.description: Lists all connected USB devices in a tree layout. Shows device name, manufacturer, and USB version. Useful for identifying connected hardware.

commands.title: Show laptop battery status
commands.description: Shows detailed battery information: charge level, capacity, charge rate, and health. The path may vary — try ls /sys/class/power_supply/ to find the right name.

commands.title: Check disk SMART health status
commands.description: Reads SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) data from a disk to check its health. Warns if the disk is showing signs of failure. Replace /dev/sda with your drive.

commands.title: Show logs from current boot
commands.description: Shows all system log messages from the current boot session. journalctl is the primary way to read logs on systemd systems. Use -p err to show only errors.

commands.title: Follow logs in real time
commands.description: Streams system logs in real time — like 'tail -f' but for the entire system journal. Great for watching what happens when you trigger an event.

commands.title: Show logs for a specific service
commands.description: Shows log output from a specific systemd service. Add -f to follow in real time, or -n 50 to show only the last 50 lines. Replace nginx with any service name.

commands.title: Show only error-level system logs
commands.description: Filters journal to show only errors and critical messages (priority 0-3). Great for a quick health check on a server to see if anything is going wrong.

commands.title: Show logs between two timestamps
commands.description: Shows logs within a specific time range. Times can be absolute (2024-01-01 12:00:00) or relative (--since '1 hour ago'). Very useful for incident investigation.

commands.title: Check journal disk usage
commands.description: Shows how much disk space the journal is using and the configured limits. Use 'sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M' to reduce journal size to 500 MB.

commands.title: Manually run logrotate
commands.description: Forces logrotate to run immediately, rotating and compressing log files. Normally runs via cron. -v shows verbose output. Useful for testing logrotate configs.

commands.title: Show recent authentication failures
commands.description: Shows recent failed SSH login attempts and sudo failures from the auth log. Essential for spotting brute force attacks. Also check: journalctl -u sshd | grep Failed

commands.title: Show kernel ring buffer messages (dmesg)
commands.description: Shows messages from the kernel ring buffer — hardware events, driver messages, boot messages, USB connections. dmesg -w follows new messages in real time. dmesg -T shows human-readable timestamps.

commands.title: Install logwatch (automated log analysis)
commands.description: Installs logwatch, which sends a daily email digest summarising important log events. Useful on servers to get a daily overview of what's happening.
commands.command: sudo apt install logwatch && sudo logwatch --output stdout --range today

commands.title: Install Flatpak support
commands.description: Installs Flatpak and adds the Flathub repository — the largest source of Flatpak apps. Flatpak apps run in a sandbox and work on any Linux distro.
commands.command: sudo apt install flatpak && flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo

commands.title: Search for a Flatpak app
commands.description: Searches Flathub for apps matching a name. Shows the app ID needed to install it.

commands.title: Install a Flatpak app from Flathub
commands.description: Installs an app from Flathub. The full app ID (e.g. org.mozilla.firefox) is used to identify apps. Find IDs with 'flatpak search' or on flathub.org.

commands.title: Update all Flatpak apps
commands.description: Updates all installed Flatpak applications to their latest versions. Flatpak apps update independently from system packages.

commands.title: List installed Flatpak apps
commands.description: Lists all installed Flatpak applications with their names, app IDs, and versions.

commands.title: Install a snap package
commands.description: Installs an app from the Snap Store. Snaps are self-contained packages that work on any Linux distro with snapd installed. --classic allows full system access for developer tools.

commands.title: List installed snap packages
commands.description: Lists all installed snap packages with their versions and channels.

commands.title: Update all snap packages
commands.description: Updates all installed snap packages to their latest versions. Snaps auto-update in the background, but this forces an immediate update.

commands.title: Make an AppImage executable and run it
commands.description: Makes an AppImage file executable and runs it. AppImages are portable apps that run without installation. Always check the source before running downloaded AppImages.

commands.title: Integrate AppImage into app menu
commands.description: Installs appimaged — a daemon that automatically adds AppImages in ~/Applications to your app launcher when you place them there. Makes AppImages work like installed apps.

commands.title: Install Wine (run Windows apps)
commands.description: Installs Wine — lets you run Windows .exe programs on Linux. winehq-stable is the most compatible version for everyday Windows apps and many games.
commands.command: sudo dpkg --add-architecture i386 && sudo apt update && sudo apt install wine wine32 wine64

commands.title: Run a Windows .exe with Wine
commands.description: Launches a Windows executable with Wine. Wine creates a 'wineprefix' (virtual C: drive) at ~/.wine the first time. Many Windows apps and games run without any tweaks.

commands.title: Install jq (JSON processor)
commands.description: Installs jq — the essential command-line tool for working with JSON. Slice, filter, map, and transform JSON data. Found on almost every production server.

commands.title: Pretty-print JSON with jq
commands.description: Formats and colourises JSON for readability. The '.' filter is identity — passes everything through but with pretty formatting. Pipe any JSON output into jq for instant readability.

commands.title: Extract a JSON field with jq
commands.description: Extracts a specific field from JSON. .name gets the 'name' key. .items[0] gets the first item of an array. .user.email navigates nested objects.

commands.title: Filter a JSON array with jq
commands.description: Selects items from a JSON array that match a condition. .[] iterates the array, select() filters items, and the result is an array of matching items.

commands.title: Transform JSON structure with jq
commands.description: Reshapes JSON by constructing a new object from selected fields. Very useful for extracting only the fields you need from a complex API response.

commands.title: Convert JSON array to CSV (jq)
commands.description: Converts a JSON array of objects to CSV format. @csv formats an array as a CSV line. Replace the field list with your actual field names.

commands.title: Install yq (YAML processor)
commands.description: Installs yq — like jq but for YAML files. Also handles JSON, TOML, and XML. Essential for working with Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files, and Ansible playbooks.

commands.title: Read a YAML field with yq
commands.description: Reads a specific field from a YAML file using yq. Uses the same dot notation as jq. Great for scripting with Kubernetes manifests or any YAML config file.

commands.title: Edit a YAML value in-place with yq
commands.description: Modifies a field in a YAML file in-place without corrupting formatting. -i modifies the file directly. Useful for scripting configuration changes.

commands.title: Install csvkit (CSV tools)
commands.description: Installs csvkit — a collection of tools for working with CSV files in the terminal. Includes csvstat (statistics), csvcut (columns), csvgrep (filter), csvsql (SQL queries on CSV), and csvjson.

commands.title: Show CSV file statistics
commands.description: Displays statistics for each column in a CSV file: min, max, mean, median, most common values. Great for getting a quick overview of any dataset.

commands.title: Run SQL query on a CSV file
commands.description: Runs SQL queries directly on CSV files as if they were database tables — no database needed. Supports SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, JOIN (between multiple CSV files), etc.
commands.command: csvsql --query 'SELECT name, age FROM data WHERE age > 30 ORDER BY age' data.csv

commands.title: Stash uncommitted changes
commands.description: Saves your current working changes to a temporary stash without committing, so you can switch branches or pull without conflicts. 'git stash pop' restores them.
commands.command: git stash push -m "description of what I was doing"

commands.title: Restore stashed changes
commands.description: Applies the most recent stash back to your working directory. 'git stash list' shows all stashes. 'git stash apply stash@{1}' applies a specific one.

commands.title: Cherry-pick a commit from another branch
commands.description: Applies a specific commit from any branch onto the current branch. Replace the hash with the commit hash you want (from git log). Useful for backporting fixes.

commands.title: Interactive rebase (squash, reorder commits)
commands.description: Opens an interactive editor to squash, reorder, rename, or drop commits. HEAD~5 means the last 5 commits. Change 'pick' to 'squash' to combine with the previous commit.

commands.title: Find the commit that introduced a bug (bisect)
commands.description: Uses binary search through commit history to find the exact commit that introduced a bug. You mark commits as good or bad — git bisect narrows it down logarithmically.
commands.command: git bisect start && git bisect bad HEAD && git bisect good v1.0.0

commands.title: Show git history as a graph
commands.description: Displays git history as a colorised ASCII graph with branch visualization. --oneline shows one commit per line, --decorate shows branch/tag names. Great for understanding branch structure.

commands.title: See who last modified each line (blame)
commands.description: Shows the author and commit for each line in a file. Useful for understanding why a line exists and who to ask about it. -L 10,20 limits to lines 10-20.

commands.title: View git reflog (undo mistakes)
commands.description: Shows a history of where HEAD has been — including commits that were 'deleted' by reset or rebase. Essential for recovering lost commits. Use 'git checkout <hash>' to rescue them.

commands.title: Create a git worktree (work on two branches)
commands.description: Creates a second working directory for the same repo at a different branch. Work on two branches simultaneously without stashing or committing. 'git worktree list' shows all.

commands.title: Create a pre-commit hook
commands.description: Creates a pre-commit hook script that runs before every commit. Exit with non-zero to reject the commit. Use this to run tests, linting, or other checks automatically.

commands.title: Add a git submodule
commands.description: Adds another git repository as a subdirectory within your repo. Common for including shared libraries or dependencies. 'git submodule update --init --recursive' initialises cloned repos.
